documents.abstract: This study aims to identify the body segments that predominantly experience musculoskeletal complaints and determine the level of ergonomic risk among Fresh Fruit Bunch (FFB) harvesters at a smallholder oil palm plantation in Rampoang Village, Tanalili District, North Luwu Regency. This study employed a descriptive design with quantitative and qualitative approaches. The sample was determined using the Total Sampling technique, involving all five permanent harvesters. Data were collected through work posture observation and a standardized Nordic Body Map (NBM) questionnaire measuring subjective complaints across 28 body segments. The results showed that the most dominant complaints occurred in the upper neck (85%), lower back (75%), right and left upper arms (65% each), and back (60%). These complaints were associated with awkward work postures, including extreme neck hyperextension when cutting fronds and fruit at heights of 4–7 meters and extreme trunk flexion when collecting loose fruit. Based on the accumulated NBM scores, 80% of workers (4 people) were classified as having a Low Risk Level with scores ranging from 45 to 48, while 20% (1 person) were classified as having a Moderate Risk Level with a score of 55. The findings indicate that FFB harvesting activities involve physical workloads concentrated in the upper and middle parts of the body. Although the current ergonomic risk level is predominantly low to moderate, improvements in work methods and regular muscle stretching are necessary to prevent the worsening of musculoskeletal injuries in the future.

documents.abstract: This academic presentation examines the challenges of ensuring secure, reliable, and energy-efficient operation in Internet of Battle Things (IoBT) environments, where heterogeneous sensors, autonomous systems, and mobile nodes must exchange critical information under resource constraints, unstable connectivity, and increased exposure to cyber threats. Drawing upon a critical review and comparative synthesis of relevant scientific literature, the study introduces ARGUS, a conceptual, multi-layered Edge–Fog–Cloud architecture for secure and resilient multimodal sensor fusion. The proposed framework integrates IoBT and Internet of Digital Twins (IoDT) concepts with AI-based sensing, Zero Trust principles, continuous trust assessment, and dynamic isolation of suspicious or compromised nodes. Particular emphasis is placed on the Fog/Trust Gateway, which coordinates local data processing, anomaly detection, security policy enforcement, and the selective transmission of verified information to higher-level analytical and decision-support systems. The name ARGUS draws inspiration from Argus Panoptes, the many-eyed guardian of Greek mythology, symbolizing continuous vigilance, distributed situational awareness, and security monitoring across the infrastructure. The study further examines energy-aware and trust-aware routing, UAV-assisted data collection, network resilience, and the operational trade-offs between energy efficiency, communication performance, and security. Through a structured qualitative comparison of existing technological approaches, it highlights their complementary capabilities and limitations, positioning ARGUS as an integrated theoretical framework for future IoBT/IoDT infrastructures. Developed within the academic framework of the course “Mobile and Pervasive Computing” at the Department of Applied Informatics, University of Macedonia, this presentation offers a literature-based architectural proposal intended to support further research into secure, intelligent, and resilient distributed systems, including their potential evolution toward 2030 and beyond.

This study examined how mature female learners sustained postgraduate study while working full time and raising families, a topic with few qualitative accounts in the Philippine teaching profession. Using a qualitative case study design bounded by the participants’ shared characteristics, and institutional contexts, the researchers conducted three individual semi-structured interviews and one focus group discussion with three married mothers employed as teachers in different institutional contexts. Self-Determination Theory, Feminist Theory, and the Chain of Response Model guided the interpretation of motivation, gendered constraints, and barriers to adult participation. Thematic analysis showed that participants faced time scarcity, work-related demands, financial pressure, and technological and cognitive challenges associated with age. They sustained their studies through disciplined time management, task prioritization, brief and purposeful distraction, support from family, colleagues, and administrators, and a positive attitude. Responsive and personalized academic advising emerged as a critical institutional factor that strengthened motivation, maintained momentum, and supported progress toward degree completion. Participants also valued flexible learning modalities, empathetic faculty, and structured check-ins. The findings illustrate how intrinsic motivation, resilience, and strategic coping interact with structural support to enable persistence. Interpreted through the three frameworks, participants’ needs for autonomy, competence, and relatedness were supported or strained by situational, institutional, and dispositional conditions, and caregiving was redistributed among family members rather than removed. Because the case involved only three participants, the findings are offered for analytic transferability, not statistical generalization. The study recommends that higher education institutions, academic advisers, and policymakers provide flexible scheduling, financial assistance, and proactive advisory services that recognize the gendered and situational constraints faced by mature female learners.

In recent years, among students of leading universities, there has been an alarming dynamics of deterioration of their psychological state, which is expressed, among other things, in the suicidal behavior of students. Indicators of subjective well-being and internal motivation of students are not only at a low level, but also continue to decline with each year of study, while according to the self-determination theory, high efficiency (providing the ability to study in a highly selective university) should be supported by exactly these factors. In connection with this contradiction, the question arises: is the influence of subjective well-being and motivation on a person's success as unambiguous as it is commonly believed, or are there different profiles of motivational and emotional regulation that allow you to gain high achievements? This article is devoted to the study of the impact of the relationship between subjective well-being and various types of academic motivation on the level of academic achievements. The results of cluster and comparative analysis of the obtained data are presented. The sample of the study consisted of 209 students of bachelor's and master's degrees of various specialties of HSE. Statistical analysis showed that combinations of negative affect with extrinsic motivation and positive affect with intrinsic motivation contribute to the formation of two alternative profiles that do not affect academic success and involvement, but are reflected in the level of student well-being. It is noteworthy that the distinctive characteristics of students with high academic performance are high motivation for achievement and low negative affect. The problematic issues of well-being and motivation in the academic environment are discussed, the question of the problematic nature of external motivation in the university for the well-being of students is raised.

The unprecedented growth in artificial intelligence and data center energy demand has renewed interest in small modular reactors (SMRs) as a potential low-carbon baseload solution. Yet significant uncertainty persists around the techno-economic characteristics and policy solutions necessary for SMR commercialization in the United States. This inadvertently leaves policymakers navigating critical decisions about resource allocation, regulatory reform, and long-term energy planning without a clear picture of near-term prospects of SMRs. This study addresses that gap by conducting a mixed methods expert survey of 33 professionals from industry, academia, government, utilities, and think tanks. Results collectively suggest a moderate confidence in an outlook with high overnight capital cost of over $6000/kW and cost overruns of over 30%, falling short of DOE's commercialization target. They also reflect cautious optimism rooted in the expectation of an incremental learning rate due to rapid electricity demand growth from data centers and standardization of design. Overall, experts highlight a significant gap between promotional narratives and realistic techno-economic trajectories.

As large language models (LLMs) increasingly power financial conversational assistants, detecting investment advice in natural language has become a critical regulatory and safety challenge. Unlike explicit single-turn recommendations, investment advice often emerges implicitly and progressively over multi-turn conversations, shaped by user intent, delivery style, and contextual buildup. We introduce the first comprehensive framework for detecting both sequential and contextual investment advice in dialogue settings. Central to our approach is a modular, top-down synthetic data generation pipeline that systematically spans a taxonomy of advisory trajectories using an axis-bucket-descriptor schema. We simulate both benign and high-risk conversations across diverse user personas, financial instruments, and risk tiers, and evaluate detection capabilities using LLM-as-a-Judge with entropy-based uncertainty diagnostics. Our results show that contextual advisory detection remains substantially more challenging than sequential cases, even under few-shot prompting with tailored demonstrations. This work lays the foundation for scalable guardrail development in high-stakes, compliance-sensitive domains, where advisory risk is often subtle, distributed, and perception-dependent.

Purpose Generative AI changes the radiologist's task from judging AI output to editing and signing text that AI drafted. Existing guidance covers automation bias, local validation and monitoring, but gives little direction on verifying generated text, recording its provenance, or auditing reliance on it. Approach This paper consolidates multisociety statements, consensus guidelines, human-factors evidence and the EU legal framework as of October 2026 into a practice framework, and applies it to assistive, case-allocation, autonomous and generative workflows. Framework PRIME has five principles at two levels. Primacy of accountability, rigorous verification and maintained expertise apply to the radiologist; informed transparency and earned trust through oversight apply to the institution. A recorded independent read before AI output is viewed links four principles: it serves as the omission search, keeps unassisted skill in routine work, supplies the data for reliance metrics, and documents the radiologist's own judgment. Verification is split into checking AI statements and searching for omissions. Provenance is recorded per statement and paired with local performance data. Monitoring uses an independent reference sample, because audits against the signed report miss errors that radiologists accepted. Implications Each principle names an actor, an action, an indicator and a trigger, and is mapped to the AI Act, the Medical Device Regulation, the General Data Protection Regulation and product liability law. Most rules are design proposals that still require clinical evaluation, and the framework does not resolve liability or structural inequity.

documents.abstract: Voluntary corporate transparency seeks to promote accountability through disclosure, but substantive reporting does not by itself guarantee societal benefits. We examine whether this form of self-regulation can help curb corruption where formal oversight is weak, focusing on corporate support for the Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (EITI), a multistakeholder initiative that promotes disclosure of company payments to host governments. We link geolocated data on African oil and gas fields and their operators to Afrobarometer surveys and satellite nighttime-light measures and estimate difference-in-differences models that track changes in outcomes around the same fields before and after operators endorse the EITI. We find that corporate EITI support is associated with lower perceived corruption and less reported bribery, greater civic engagement, greater perceived freedom to speak, and higher nighttime-light intensity, a proxy for local economic activity. The association with lower perceived corruption is stronger around fields with nearby NGO or aid-project activity, among residents living closer to fields, and among frequent users of traditional news media. Supplementary analyses provide indirect evidence that supporting firms were more transparent before mandatory disclosure laws took effect, and show that they had fewer joint-venture partners and larger ownership stakes after endorsement. Archival cases from Nigeria and Ghana illustrate how civil-society organizations and journalists use extractive-industry information to question firms and public authorities. The findings point to local governance benefits of voluntary transparency commitments and are consistent with an information-to-accountability account in which these benefits depend on both substantive reporting and local opportunities to scrutinize and use the information.

Increasingly, physicians must oversee AI systems to detect system malfunctions. We studied 48 physicians in a randomized controlled study using an increasingly malfunctioning AI for cardiac auscultation. Diagnostic performance declined alongside AI reliability, even when physicians were cognitively forced to make an initial classification, and when human performance exceeded AI reliability. Physicians' confidence declined faster than their trust in AI. Results call for specification of oversight goals and processes ensuring patient safety.

documents.abstract: This article analyzes the peculiarities of choosing and considering body shapes when creating modern clothing designs, exploring its artistic-constructive and socio-psychological aspects. In the contemporary fashion industry, couturiers and designers no longer limit themselves to standard templates; instead, they focus heavily on the plasticity, proportions, and visual correction of diverse body structures. The article provides a theoretical and scientific justification for the role of lines, fabric textures, color harmony, and constructive solutions in garment design for various body types. Furthermore, it highlights the principles of creating ergonomically and aesthetically flawless garments by ensuring a harmonious balance between the consumer's individual identity and physical form. The study also considers the methodological stages of the design process, the influence of age and cultural context, the relationship between sizing systems and body morphology, and the growing importance of inclusivity and sustainability in contemporary fashion.

This article examines the motivations that drive Cleopatra to fight against her brother, Ptolemy, in H. Rider Haggard’s Cleopatra (1889). The study develops a qualitative literary analysis of the novel through close attention to dialogue, character action, political decisions, and recurring patterns of conflict. The analysis distinguishes between intrinsic motivation and power motivation and then examines how these dimensions intersect rather than operate independently. The findings identify two major intrinsic motives—desire for Egyptian independence and concern for legacy and dynastic continuity—and five major power motives: political ambition, personal rivalry, strategic calculation, manipulation and control, and personal survival. Empirical textual evidence shows that these motives are repeatedly converted into concrete political practices, including mobilizing Egyptians, preparing military forces, seeking alliances, approaching Julius Caesar, challenging Ptolemy’s legitimacy, manipulating factions, and protecting Cleopatra’s political position. The discussion demonstrates that national sovereignty and personal ambition are not mutually exclusive within the novel: Cleopatra presents the consolidation of her authority as a means of securing Egypt’s future, while her pursuit of sovereignty simultaneously strengthens her personal power. Maslow’s hierarchy of needs is employed cautiously as an interpretive framework. Recent empirical research challenges the assumption that human needs are universally satisfied in a fixed sequence, supporting a more integrated interpretation of Cleopatra’s simultaneous pursuit of security, belonging, esteem, agency, and self-realization.

This chapter discusses how students co-constructed knowledge in group-work discussions using their critical thinking at a private Japanese university in Tokyo. A cognitive interactional approach was employed to investigate how students’ interactions in group-work in a CLIL classroom enhanced cognitive engagement. The audio data of students’ interactions on the function of robots in society were analysed with the two-layered framework including cognitive discourse functions (CDFs) and discourse moves. The findings show that the group discussions developed in three steps: brainstorming by describing and categorising, critical evaluation, and exploration by expanding on a previous speaker’s contribution. The implication is that these three steps are crucial in bringing about students’ thinking in a collaborative way to encourage cognitive engagement in students’ interaction. The data show that the CDFs, Evaluate and Describe acted as a trigger for the critical dialogic inquiry to occur in the group-work discussions.

This study examines the connections between information literacy and Media and AI Literacy (MAIL), investigating the latter as a possible sociotechnical expansion of the former. It adopts a qualitative, exploratory, bibliographic, and documentary approach, complemented by a descriptive survey of 828 publications retrieved from BRAPCI between 1985 and 2026. Results indicate recent growth in AI-related research, the persistence of core Information Science concepts, and convergences regarding critical evaluation, ethics, autonomy, civic participation, and lifelong learning. The study concludes that MAIL broadens information literacy by incorporating algorithms, data, automated systems, and synthetic content. It proposes the CoInfo-AI framework for artificial intelligence ecosystems.

This chapter examines the technological interface from a sociotechnical and interdisciplinary perspective.It describes the shift from the functionalist paradigm, which valued products by algorithmic performance, electronic stability and compliance with technical requirements, towards user-centred design, which holds that interactive systems must adapt to people's needs, cognitive limitations and contexts of use.Within this framework, usability and aesthetics are presented not as ornamental or independent attributes but as dimensions to be integrated.The chapter treats hardware and software as a single sociotechnical system: hardware provides the material canvas in which aesthetics first appears, while software shapes the interactive dynamics in which usability is experienced.The graphical user interface (GUI) is therefore addressed as the core of interaction, the space where functional and visual attributes converge.The approach is a conceptual, descriptive-analytical review of human-computer interaction literature, covering event-driven programming and GUI components such as icons, windows, pointing devices, menus and buttons, together with a brief historical account from Xerox PARC to the Macintosh and touchscreen devices.Drawing on this literature, the chapter states that interfaces based on visual metaphors and icons reduce the learning curve and cognitive load, and that an imbalance between hardware and software quickly undermines both aesthetics and actual usability.It concludes that a holistic, interactive approach grounded in user needs is required for products to be competitive, with user-centred design proposed as the framework for integrating usability and aesthetics in organizational settings.

Large language models (LLMs) in financial applications fail most consequentially when they are confidently wrong. Hedged, uncertain answers invite scrutiny, whereas confident errors silently degrade downstream decisions without warning. We ask how reliably such confidently wrong answers, or confident hallucinations, can be detected from a model’s internal activations, and whether those activations carry information beyond its output-level confidence signals. We train linear probes on the residual stream and evaluate them on two established numerical question-answering (QA) benchmarks built from real filings, FinQA and TAT-QA. Behavioral confidence is measured as the agreement among eight resampled answers to the same question, and probe effectiveness is compared against baselines, such as token log-probabilities and the model’s own True/False self-assessment of its answer. Our findings show that among confident answers, those for which all eight resamples agree, 15–23% are wrong on FinQA. There the probes have a significant advantage over output-level baselines in detecting hallucinations, holding 0.68–0.77 AUROC while the best baselines fall to 0.55–0.63, across Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B, and Gemma-2-9B. Our results suggest that probing can be a cost-effective triage mechanism for routing LLM answers to human review and quality control procedures in high-stakes financial applications. Code and data are available at https://github.com/richardzhewang/confidently-wrong.

Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) shapes content to increase its likelihood of being cited by answer engines built on retrieval-augmented large language models. GEO is typically evaluated as a single-turn property: for a fixed query, an evaluator measures a source’s visibility in one answer. We argue that the single answer is an inadequate unit of analysis. Human-agent information seeking forms a closed loop. The agent’s answer changes the user’s beliefs and therefore the next question, which in turn determines what the agent retrieves. We introduce conversational capture, a phenomenon in which a source cited early becomes substantially more likely to be cited again. Capture operates through a machine-side channel, history-conditioned retrieval, and a human-side channel, follow-up questions directed toward the captured source. This persistence can be independent of the source’s current relevance. We formalize the interaction as a two-layer closed-loop system and derive computable trajectory-level constructs: cumulative conversational visibility; a decomposition of trajectory gain into a single-turn "direct" term and a closed-loop "feedback" term; a nested counterfactual split of the feedback term into machine-side and human-side channels; a capture coefficient; a compounding ratio; and a misranking diagnostic. Using reinforcement-process (Pólya-urn) theory, we prove that the feedback term is identically zero under single-turn evaluation and that GEO’s cumulative payoff grows superlinearly with conversation length while capture develops. A model-derived illustration shows that the feedback term can exceed the direct term, the compounding ratio exceeds two within ten turns, and the single-turn and trajectory rankings of GEO methods agree only weakly (Kendall’s τ = 0.4). Thus, single-turn evaluation can select the wrong method. We connect the human channel to information foraging, trust calibration, and Bayesian persuasion, and discuss design implications for answer engines.

Real-time strategy (RTS) games represent challenging simulation environments for many decision-making algorithms due to their large state and action spaces, limited decision times, a partially known environment, and different human opponents. The most used methods are based on scripting, finite-state machines (FSM), or behaviour trees and have been successfully integrated into game engines such as Unreal Engine or Unity. However, these methods can suffer from redundant and predictable actions, thus reducing player immersion. Furthermore, it is very hard to maintain or evolve these techniques when the state space becomes large. The approach described in this chapter overcomes these limitations by providing a better ergonomic game artificial intelligence (AI) architecture. The code is more structured, reusable, and maintainable by partitioning it into four distinct components: Perception, Strategical AI (Macro), Tactical AI(Squad), and Unit FSM.

This study discursively analyzes the video “Adultização”, produced by the influencer Felipe Bressanim Pereira (Felca), with the aim of understanding the construction of discursive authority and its effects on the processes of information circulation and legitimation in sociotechnical contexts. Linked to the field of Information Science, the study discusses the role of digital influencers on platforms characterized by dynamics of visibility, engagement, and algorithmic mediation, highlighting the impacts produced by these structures on the organization of informational flows. The research adopts a qualitative approach grounded in the discourse analysis proposed by Orlandi (2015), articulated with the concepts of informational practices, information mediation, and platform governance. The results reveal the influencer as a subject capable of mobilizing audiences, using visibility to promote public debates and problematize dynamics related to information circulation and legitimacy in digital environments. It is concluded that Felca’s performance goes beyond the dissemination of content, positioning him as an informational subject capable of disputing meanings and tensioning dynamics of visibility and monetization on digital platforms.

Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly embedded into applications, allowing users to complete tasks either through direct manipulation or by delegating actions to conversational agents. However, little is known about how users balance these modalities when both are available. We present a web-based content management system augmented with an LLM agent through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), enabling users to perform CRUD tasks through a graphical interface, a conversational agent, or both. We conducted a between-subjects study (N=73) comparing three interaction modes: Traditional-Only, AI-First, and Hybrid. Across sixteen scenarios, we analyzed task completion time, interaction logs, and delegation behavior. AI-assisted interaction significantly reduced clicks, page navigations, and scrolling, indicating lower interaction effort. Surprisingly, these reductions did not translate into faster task completion, as task duration did not differ significantly across conditions. We also found no significant relationship between CRUD operation type and delegation, suggesting that users did not systematically avoid delegating higher-risk actions. Instead, delegation varied far more between participants than between tasks, with individual differences accounting for roughly half the variance in assistant use (ICC =.50). Our findings suggest that the primary benefit of human–agent interfaces may be reducing interaction effort rather than improving speed, and that delegation reflects who the user is more than what the task demands.

Background: Manual handling during wheelchair loading and unloading imposes substantial biomechanical demands on caregivers, potentially contributing to work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs) because of non-neutral working postures and increased spinal loading, particularly at the L5/S1 lumbosacral junction. Objective: This study proposes the design, development, and ergonomic evaluation of an electromechanical assistive lifting device integrated into the cargo compartment of a Toyota Avanza multipurpose vehicle (MPV). Methods: A 12-V DC electric winch equipped with a swiveling boom arm and a quick-release sling harness was evaluated during caregiver-assisted wheelchair loading and unloading tasks involving three wheelchair configurations: a standard manual wheelchair (17 kg), a Type A powered wheelchair, and a Type B powered wheelchair (weighing up to 28 kg). Functional compatibility and observable caregiver working postures were assessed before and after device implementation. Results: Automated lifting system successfully demonstrated proof-of-concept operation with all three wheelchair configurations. Compared with manual handling, assisted loading reduced the need for non-neutral caregiver postures, including approximately 30° of backward trunk extension and approximately 75° of asymmetric lower-extremity bracing. By replacing manual lifting effort with electromechanical assistance, the device enabled the caregiver to maintain a more upright working posture during the demonstrated operations. However, repeated trial counts were not documented; therefore, no statistical success rate or quantified reduction in biomechanical loading can be established. Conclusion: Proof-of-concept device demonstrated functional feasibility and the potential to reduce non-neutral caregiver postures during wheelchair loading and unloading. Its integration into the vehicle cargo compartment offers a practical retrofit concept for assisted wheelchair transportation.

documents.abstract: Conventional domestic entry notification frameworks rely predominantly on acoustic propagation, presenting an institutionalized accessibility barrier for the deaf and hard-of-hearing demographic. While localized visual or haptic retrofitting solutions exist for permanent installations, they remain highly impractical for transitory, short-term rental, or travel accommodations where structural and electrical grid modifications are legally or structurally prohibited. This paper presents a novel, grid-independent, non-destructive assistive telemetry node designed specifically for temporary or mobile spatial environments. Utilizing a RISC-V based ESP32-C3 microcontroller, the system circumvents local spatial constraints by routing hardware-interrupt-driven trigger events over an automated network captive portal directly to a secure cloud broker (Telegram Bot API). The alert payload is translated at the user's mobile endpoint into multi-modal haptic-visual feedback streams, ensuring unconstrained geographical tracking. The hardware layer is packaged inside a custom additive-manufactured Polyethylene Terephthalate Glycol (PETG) enclosure optimized for rugged field mobility and tool-free deployment. Electrical characterization yields an optimized deep-sleep quiescent current floor of 7.2µA sustained via an ultra-low-power low-dropout (LDO) linear regulator stage. Empirical evaluations across eighteen distinct evaluation iterations demonstrate an overall mean end-to-end network latency of 5.86 seconds and a 100% transmission success rate, translating to a mathematically validated operational battery deployment shelf-life exceeding 14 to 16 months on standard commercial alkaline cells. Qualitative field evaluations with an assistive user cohort verify that the multi-modal notification pipeline significantly enhances situational awareness and independent living capacity without technical onboarding friction.

Awkward working postures pose ergonomic risks in industrial workshops, particularly when combined with force, repetition, or prolonged exposure. This study implements a human-in-the-loop ergonomic assessment system integrating MediaPipe Pose, Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA), and edge computing. A Jetson Orin Nano processes uploaded media and Real Time Streaming Protocol (RTSP) camera streams. MediaPipe estimates 33 body landmarks to calculate six segment angles, while HSE personnel verify landmark placement and task factors before final scoring. The system stores assessment records in MySQL and displays them through a web dashboard. Four workshop postures involving low-workpiece handling, pipe maintenance, grinding, and welding demonstrate system functionality. System-derived REBA scores were 5 for squatting (Case A) and conditionally 5 for bending (Case B). Case B's final score was withheld because wrist visibility fell below 0.50. Observer scores were 7 and 5, respectively, with both cases classified as medium risk. Grinding and welding cases were evaluated without observer comparisons. Segment agreement reached 3/5 for Case A and 5/5 for Case B. During a two-hour RTSP test involving 93,729 frames, mean latency was 74.14 ± 19.64 ms, throughput reached 13.04 ± 2.08 FPS, and CPU/GPU utilization averaged 21.35%/57.71%. Findings demonstrate operational feasibility while identifying hip-landmark placement and occlusion as key sensitivity factors. However, these descriptive results neither establish measurement accuracy nor demonstrate reduced musculoskeletal disorder incidence. Further instrument-based validation across diverse postures and operating conditions remains necessary to establish measurement reliability and broader practical applicability.

Abstract Background Nurses’ participation and continuing support are important dimensions of electronic medical record (EMR) implementation. Evidence comparing these experiences across donor-funded and facility-employed nurses in Kenya is limited. This study compared reported design participation, pilot participation and ongoing training between these groups. Methods This exploratory secondary analysis used a cross-sectional, self-administered nursing survey conducted between March and May 2025. Analyses included 329 nurses: 190 reporting donor-funded project work and 139 identifying as facility employed without donor-funded project work. Design participation was the primary outcome; pilot participation and ongoing training and sensitisation were secondary outcomes. Agreement combined agree and strongly agree responses. Modified Poisson regression estimated prevalence ratios (PRs) with facility-clustered robust standard errors, adjusting for gender, age, education and facility tenure. Sensitivity analyses examined alternative sample definitions and modelling approaches. Results Agreement with design participation was 26.3% among donor-funded respondents and 47.5% among facility-employed respondents; corresponding proportions were 43.7% and 69.8% for pilot participation, and 96.8% and 55.4% for ongoing training. After adjustment, differences in design participation (PR 0.85, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.53–1.34) and pilot participation (PR 0.87, 95% CI 0.65–1.16) attenuated. Higher agreement with ongoing training persisted (PR 1.83, 95% CI 1.49–2.26), with consistent findings across sensitivity analyses. All respondents agreed with deployment training. Non-agreement with ongoing training among facility-employed respondents was predominantly neutral. Conclusions Work affiliation was associated with reported ongoing EMR training, while adjusted differences in design and pilot participation remained uncertain. Nursing managers should assess continuing support separately from deployment training and review training opportunities across work affiliations. These exploratory associations do not establish causal effects of employment or donor funding.

Contact dermatitis (CD) plays a significant role in occupational health due to its frequent occurrence and environmental triggers and is among the most common occupational diseases in Western countries. Despite its prevalence, occupational contact dermatitis (OCD) is often overlooked by occupational physicians, largely due to limited knowledge and a lack of validated detection tools. Advances in digital technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) offer promising opportunities for improving early detection, yet an overview of available digital tools and their effectiveness in dermatitis detection is lacking. A systematic review was conducted in PubMed, Embase, Cinahl, and Scopus. The search focused on original studies published in peer-reviewed journals between 2014 and 2024. Forty-three studies evaluating digital tools for dermatitis detection were included, categorized as models (n = 31) or devices (n = 12). Models represent AI algorithms not yet in practical use, while devices are tools already implemented. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) were the most commonly used computational technique. Median sensitivity and specificity were 0.84 and 0.97 for all tools, 0.85 and 0.97 for models, and 0.78 and 0.97 for devices. The results provided in this review will serve as valuable input for the development of new tools to enhance early OCD detection.

Digital twins (DTs) are increasingly proposed as a pathway toward safer, more adaptive, and more efficient intersection management, yet the literature remains conceptually uneven and methodologically fragmented. This review critically synthesizes 99 studies on DTs and closely related DT-enabling systems for intelligent intersections through five analytical dimensions, namely (i) Architectures and Integration Frameworks, (ii) Data Pipelines and Simulation Fidelity, (iii) Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning (AI/ML) for Twin-Enabled Traffic Control, (iv) Human-Centered Safety, Vulnerable Road Users (VRUs), and Ethics, and (v) Scaling, Orchestration, and Network Integration. The review adopts a human-curated, multi-source screening and synthesis process in which large language models (LLMs) are used as bounded support tools for note taking, early screening, and draft synthesis, while all final interpretations, categorizations, and claims are validated against the source texts. Beyond summarizing recent work, the paper explicitly distinguishes digital models, digital shadows, and twin-complete systems, showing that many self-labeled transportation “digital twins” exhibit characteristics more consistent with digital shadows or advanced simulators, with only a smaller subset demonstrating operationally coupled twin functionality. The synthesis highlights major advances in modular architectures, multimodal sensing, co-simulation, reinforcement learning, and edge-to-cloud deployment, while also identifying persistent gaps in bidirectional synchronization, validation under real-world uncertainty, VRU-centered design, interoperability, governance, and large-scale deployment. The paper concludes with a sharper research agenda for moving DTs for intelligent intersections from promising prototypes toward operational, trustworthy, and human-centered urban systems.

Background: Digitalization has greatly transformed HRM all over the world, especially in the field of recruitment. However, Nigerian Public Institutions still experience difficulties in the adoption and implementation of digital recruitment systems. Objective: This study explored the challenges and opportunities of digitalization in the recruitment process in the Federal Ministry of Agriculture and Food Security, Nigeria. Method: A quantitative case study was used, and data were collected from 30 human resource managers, information technology officers, and recruitment staff using a structured questionnaire given via Google Forms. The questionnaire included technical challenges, human factors, organizational factors, perceived potentials, and digital recruitment effectiveness measured on a 5-point Likert scale. Results: Descriptive results revealed moderate technical, human, and organizational challenges, while perceived potentials of digital recruitment showed higher mean scores ranging from 4.10 to 4.32, particularly for efficiency, transparency, and access to talent. Technical challenges (r = ?0.42) and human factors (r = ?0.35) were negatively correlated with digital recruitment effectiveness, whereas perceived potentials showed the strongest positive relationship (r = 0.85). Regression analysis revealed that perceived potentials had a significant positive effect (? = 0.78, p < 0.001), while technical challenges had a significant negative effect (? = ?0.35, p = 0.007). Conclusion: The findings highlight the need to improve technical infrastructure and strengthen the potential benefits of digital recruitment to facilitate more effective recruitment practices in Nigerian public institutions.

Context: As digital technologies advance rapidly, organizations require analytical frameworks that move beyond subjective intuition and interpret ease of use as a sociotechnical property that regulates business efficiency.Objective: The chapter analyzes the functional dimension of interactive design through the formalization of usability within the corporate environment of organizations.Method: An analytical-conceptual, descriptive and foundational approach was used, based on a systematic review of standards in computer ergonomics and in human-computer interaction (HCI) and on the operationalization of the construct into performance variables and indicators.The chapter examines the definition of usability provided by the ISO 9241-11 standard, its articulation with the ISO 9241-210 standard, Jakob Nielsen's five-attribute model, the conceptual distinction between usability and user experience (UX), and the operational principles of usable design in organizations.Results: According to the analysis, the systematic measurement of effectiveness, efficiency and satisfaction optimizes workflows and limits cognitive load, and these dimensions constitute the basis for the quantitative diagnosis of interaction.However, challenges remain, such as the terminological confusion between usability and UX and the difficulty of achieving operational consistency and reversibility.Conclusions: Usability is a necessary, though not sufficient, component of a competitive UX.The formal adoption of the ISO 9241-11 standard is suggested in order to reduce technical support costs, shorten users' learning curves and maximize the perceived value of the product.

Driving styles reflect the behaviours of drivers and their tendencies to drive carefully, perform riskier manoeuvres or break traffic rules. They also play a significant role in traffic safety, as how calm or aggressive a person drives can determine how likely they are to enter an unsafe scenario and potentially crash. There are a wide variety of potential applications for a system that can identify driving styles and score driving trips, such as increasing drivers’ awareness of their shortcomings and adaptive insurance policies. To tackle this topic, this paper details a trip-scoring system using a Siamese network that inputs data grouped using k-means clustering. This model can be used to measure the aggressiveness of drivers in their respective communities by comparing them to their peers in similar environments; Siamese network is a high-speed machine learning system for comparing data that will allow the inclusion of new users into the scoring system without requiring the model to be retrained every time a new user is added.
topics: IoT and GPS-based Vehicle Safety Systems

documents.abstract: Game-based learning (GBL) has interdisciplinary overlaps with media studies, and findings from educational research suggest that it can foster student engagement, critical thinking and 21st-century skills (Mao et al., 2022; Qian and Clark, 2016; Romero, Usart and Ott, 2015). However, its systematic adoption in formal K-12 education remains relatively low, particularly in the Slovak education system. This paper examines pedagogical acceptance of, and barriers to, the adoption of digital games among teachers in the regional education system of the Slovak Republic. The conceptual framework combines three complementary theoretical perspectives: Self-Determination Theory (SDT), which explains students’ intrinsic motivation through the fulfilment of psychological needs; technology acceptance models (TAM/UTAUT), which address teachers’ perceived usefulness and facilitating conditions; and Ertmer’s model of first- and second-order barriers. Quantitative data were collected from a quota sample of 105 teachers via computer-assisted personal interviewing (CAPI) in collaboration with the research agency IPSOS, and were analysed descriptively, with 95% confidence intervals for the proportion of respondents selecting each option. Teachers most frequently reported increased student motivation (54.3%), creative thinking (41.0%) and digital skills development (40.0%) as benefits of digital games, which suggests that many of them consider digital games pedagogically beneficial. Among non-users (n = 60), the most frequently reported reasons for non-use were a preference for traditional assessment (41.7%), an unclear connection to learning objectives (31.7%), a traditionally oriented school system (28.3%) and insufficient technical equipment (26.7%). Affective and competence-related second-order barriers, such as fear of losing control of the class, low digital literacy or fear of losing authority, were reported by relatively few teachers. These findings suggest that non-use is associated less with teachers’ resistance to technology than with assessment practices, curricular alignment and infrastructure, areas in which teachers’ pedagogical beliefs and institutional conditions are closely intertwined. Given the cross-sectional, self-report design, the results should be regarded as indicative; they point to the potential value of policy measures that address assessment and curriculum frameworks alongside teachers’ professional development.

ObjectiveThis study aims to investigate how the use of virtual reality (VR) and different cueing elements within VR affect individuals' scale cognition performance, workload, and visual behavior.BackgroundScale cognition refers to the ability to conceptualize spatial, temporal, and quantitative dimensions for measuring objects and processes. Although VR has shown promise in supporting various cognitive tasks, there remains a lack of research examining its effects on scale cognition. Moreover, VR-based learning may have adverse effects on users when learning environments are not carefully designed.MethodThe research team developed a VR-based learning environment, Scale Worlds, which integrated three types of cueing elements to support learning: graphic armatures, multimodal cues, and numeric measures. A between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 engineering students across five conditions: three conditions featuring individual cueing elements, one without any cueing elements, and one incorporating all cueing elements. The pre- and post-test scores of scale cognition assessment, workload, eye-movement data, and semi-structured interview data were collected and analyzed.ResultsThe VR-based learning environment significantly improved participants' scale cognition, particularly in the subscales of absolute and relative reasoning. Cueing was found to affect distinct dimensions of scale cognition, as well as cognitive engagement, visual attention, and frustration levels during learning.ConclusionVR-based learning environments can improve scale cognition, and embedded cueing elements play a modulatory role in shaping users' learning experiences.ApplicationThese findings highlight the potential of using VR to support cognitive tasks and carefully designed cues in VR to shape learning processes.

This study investigates the effects of voice and gesture interaction with in-vehicle robots on driving performance, workload, and user experience using multimodal physiological measures. A 2 (driving environment: simple vs. complex) × 3 (interaction modality: none, voice, gesture) within-subject simulated driving experiment was conducted. Eye-tracking, functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and electrocardiography (ECG) were used to record physiological responses. The results indicate that complex driving environments significantly increase cognitive and physiological demands, as reflected in higher workload, heart rate and pupil diameter, along with reduced blink frequency. The no-interaction condition was associated with lower driving workload and better driving performance. In complex environments, interaction tasks also increased ΔHbO in the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC). Although subjective evaluations favoured voice over gesture interaction, no significant differences were observed in physiological measures, whereas gesture interaction resulted in greater gaze diversion. These findings highlight the value of multimodal physiological measures for evaluating human-vehicle interaction.

The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, autonomous systems, Internet of Things (IoT), blockchain, quantum computing, and other advanced digital technologies is reshaping social institutions, economic systems, and public decision-making. These technological developments have generated new sociotechnical imaginaries—collective visions of how societies may function in AI-driven futures—and have simultaneously created complex challenges for governance, accountability, transparency, privacy, and human rights. This chapter examines the relationship between emerging technologies and AI governance by exploring how technological possibilities, institutional structures, societal expectations, and ethical values influence the development and implementation of governance frameworks. Particular attention is given to algorithmic accountability, responsible innovation, data governance, explainability, cybersecurity, regulatory adaptation, and the management of risks associated with increasingly autonomous AI systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly used in interaction design to facilitate ideation, often following their own internal reasoning. These interactions tend to expand the design space. Our work explores an antagonistic role for design agents, prompting designers to engage with stakeholder tension. We built an antagonistic AI agent and examined the agent’s influence in a between-subjects experiment with 45 design students across three conditions: Self Reflection (unsupported review of the design proposal), Stepwise Guidance (written prompts that walk designers through a constructive-conflict framework), and Interactive Engagement (an AI agent that enacts the constructive-conflict framework interactively by synthesizing stakeholder pushback). The latter two conditions share the framework but differ in whether it is self-enacted or agent-enacted. Results show that, compared with Self Reflection, both the Stepwise Guidance and Interactive Engagement groups reported significantly higher self-reconsideration and made more improvements to their design proposals. Compared with Stepwise Guidance, the antagonistic agent introduced more conflictual perspectives, and participants in the Engagement condition generated and discarded more ideas. These findings suggest that an interactive agent that surfaces stakeholder pushback can support concrete design revision while keeping designers engaged with divergent perspectives.

Recent literature on escapism in video games often categorizes escapism into healthy or unhealthy experiences. The purpose of this research was to investigate how video game players experience healthy aspects of escapism, from the perspective of previously proposed four pillars of healthy escapism framework. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 18 participants to inquire about how they experience healthy escapism. The collected qualitative data was analyzed with reflexive thematic analysis. Six interrelated themes emerged: Boundaries & Balance, Social Aspects, Empowerment, Reset & Re-entry, Recognizing Overuse, and Identity & Safe Worlds. Findings showed that healthy escapism is not only a motivation, but also a managed process. The themes extend our understanding of prior dualistic models of escapism by emphasizing the importance of setting boundaries and recognizing when habits are becoming excessive and unhealthy. This suggests that players can maintain healthy escapism through strategies such as self-monitorization and balanced approaches to gaming.

Purpose This study aims to analyze pleasure, suffering and defensive strategies among civil police officers at specialized police stations for women, based on the psychodynamics of work. Design/methodology/approach This is a qualitative study with 30 civil police officers in Ceará, Brazil. Data were collected through interviews and analyzed using sense nuclei analysis. Findings Pleasure relates to identity, recognition, practical intelligence and collaboration; suffering relates to workload, violence, institutional constraints and gender discrimination. Subjective conditions predominate. Individual defenses address suffering; collective strategies mobilize and strengthen officers but have limited capacity to prevent illness. Sisterhood emerges as resistance and collective empowerment. Practical implications Mental health monitoring, dialogue and gender equity are recommended. Social implications Findings reinforce public policies on mental health and equity. Originality/value This study extends the psychodynamics of work by highlighting the ambivalence of compensation and repression and proposing sisterhood as collective action beyond adaptation, fostering resistance and transformation.

OBJECTIVES: To establish expert consensus on the prioritization of evidence-informed safety measures for the low-noise risks of electric vehicles (EVs), and to specify consensus positions on acoustic and non-acoustic countermeasures that complement existing acoustic vehicle alerting system (AVAS) mandates. METHODS: A three-round Delphi study with 17 multidisciplinary experts (mean 17.5 years of professional experience, including a blind pedestrian expert) rated 24 items on 7-point Likert scales, and one item on a 10-point scale. Consensus required a mean absolute deviation (MAD) of 1.0 or less. The process was conducted face-to-face, so the results represent negotiated expert judgment. RESULTS: Experts agreed that low-noise EVs pose a heightened, stratified risk for vulnerable road users (VRUs), especially children, older adults and blind pedestrians (Median = 6.0; MAD = 0.2). The strongest consensus supported awareness and education campaigns (Median = 7.0; MAD = 0.1) and research into non-acoustic, system-level measures such as pedestrian detection (Median = 6.0; MAD = 0.1). Experts agreed that AVAS should sound while reversing (Median = 7.0; MAD = 0.1), not while idling (Median = 1.0; MAD = 0.6), and should vary with speed (Median = 7.0; MAD = 0.4). They recommended operation below 30 km/h, with ambient-noise adaptation, rather than only below 20 km/h as currently mandated. Simulating a combustion-engine sound, preventing driver disablement and using AVAS as a pedestrian-detection system received only moderate support (Median = 5.0; MAD = 0.5 to 0.8). Experts also identified ergonomic and psychosocial benefits of low-noise, low-vibration EVs for fleet workers. CONCLUSIONS: Negotiated expert consensus favors two near-term priorities: multi-stakeholder awareness and reeducation programmes, and selective, adaptive acoustic alerts below 30 km/h. Pedestrian detection and driver-alert systems are a promising longer-term complement that requires real-world validation before wider adoption. Findings reflect a Southern European urban context and require validation in other settings.

Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly make decisions that unfold over time: autonomous vehicles navigating traffic, robots executing manipulation sequences, game-playing agents taking moves toward their goals, and planning systems constructing multistep action sequences. Explaining such sequential behavior is fundamentally harder than explaining a single classification or regression output, yet this challenge has only recently received sustained research attention across the reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, and game-AI communities. This chapter provides an introduction to Explainable AI for Sequential Decision-Making (X-SDM). A unified taxonomy is developed that answers four core questions: what must be explained, who needs the explanation, how are explanations generated algorithmically, and how should they be evaluated. The taxonomy spans formal models including Markov Decision Processes and symbolic planning and covers the major families of explanation methods that have emerged across communities: contrastive and counterfactual explanations, feature importance and attribution methods, plan and goal explanations, model-reconciliation explanations, and intrinsically interpretable policies. These categories are illustrated with representative techniques, and a principled framework for user requirements grounded in situation-awareness theory is sketched. The chapter closes with ten open research questions that chart a roadmap for the field. The chapter integrates perspectives from reinforcement learning, AI planning, robotics, game AI, and cognitive science, offering students and researchers a structured entry point into this growing area.

Artificial intelligence (AI) offers a promising approach to governing fake news on social media, yet its effectiveness relative to human fact-checkers and the conditions shaping user acceptance remain unclear. Drawing on the Computers Are Social Actors paradigm and the Elaboration Likelihood Model, we conducted two large-scale online surveys with Chinese netizens (combined N = 3,846). Study 1 (N = 2,146) used a 2 (corrector: human vs. bot) × 2 (correction: simple tag vs. detailed rebuttal) design across 17 fake news stories. Bot-based corrections were generally as effective as human corrections; however, humans were most effective with simple tags, whereas bots required detailed rebuttals to achieve stronger outcomes. Study 2 (N = 1,700) tested news literacy and algorithm literacy interventions. Results provided partial evidence that news literacy messages improved correction effectiveness. These findings support combining AI-based corrections with critical thinking interventions to improve fake news governance.

Camera-based ergonomic screening requires continuous posture scores accompanied by explicit uncertainty. This study evaluated ErgoTCN, a causal temporal convolutional network with approximately 160,000 parameters, for estimating posture-only Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) scores from 17 simulated two-dimensional camera keypoints. Wrist posture was fixed at neutral, and load, coupling and activity inputs were excluded. Reference scores were derived from 9.8 hours of three-dimensional motion capture across 113 recorded Carnegie Mellon University subject IDs. Ten virtual camera configurations and a MoveNet-like keypoint-error model generated input streams; no real pose-detector video was assessed. Model evaluation used 28 held-out subject IDs, although distinct-person separation was unverified, and validation, calibration and test sets shared the ten camera configurations. Across three training seeds, ErgoTCN achieved a mean absolute error of 0.874 REBA points and quadratic weighted kappa of 0.781, with mean absolute error 11.1% below the gradient-boosted baseline and 18.5% below the raw-keypoint Random Forest. Empirical coverage of nominal 90% conformal intervals was 0.923, with a mean width of 3.60 scores. High-risk alert recall reached 0.744, below the target of 0.900. A random frame split increased action-level accuracy from 59.1% to 76.0%. Scoring latency was 1.24 ms per frame in PyTorch and 0.307 ms in ONNX Runtime, excluding pose detection. These results characterise simulation-based posture screening, not validated workplace performance.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) and large language model (LLM)–based simulated patients are being evaluated for problem-based learning and case-based learning in undergraduate medical education, but delivery formats are often under-specified and outcome measurement is inconsistently reported. We assessed the feasibility and acceptability of a single LLM-driven, AI-simulated patient encounter delivered in two formats—a facilitated whole-group session and a self-paced individual session—to first-year medical students (MS1), and we describe the development and provisional status of a learner-perception survey instrument. Two non-overlapping, non-randomized MS1 cohorts at one United States medical school completed the same case (Group, n = 7; Individual, n = 12) and the Behavioral Safety Language Scale–Provisional (BSLS-P) before and after the encounter. Pre-to-post change was tested with Wilcoxon signed-rank exact tests, with Benjamini–Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction across subscale comparisons. Feasibility outcomes (recruitment, encounter completion, survey completion, technical failures, and encounter duration) and acceptability outcomes (post-encounter engagement ratings, delivery-format preference, and open-ended comments) are reported descriptively. Of 72 students invited, 19 (26%) enrolled; all completed the encounter and paired pre/post surveys (100%), with no technical failures (no encounter was terminated and no participant was excluded), although learners reported intermittent technical problems that interrupted but did not end encounters; the group session lasted approximately 35 min and individual encounters a median of 31 min (range 17–83). Pre-to-post shifts were small and imprecise; in the Group cohort, median engagement changed by + 0.33 points (Wilcoxon r = 0.13, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.90). The largest effect—a psychological-safety gain in the Individual cohort (Wilcoxon r = 0.62)—was significant before correction ( P =0.026) but not after (adjusted P =0.20). No between-cohort comparison reached significance. A single motivation item declined by one median point in both cohorts. The modal post-encounter preference was a hybrid “solo first, then group” model (7/12, 58%). On the feasibility and acceptability indicators examined, the encounter was delivered as planned in both formats and was rated favorably by learners; these data do not address educational effectiveness. Observed pre-to-post shifts are exploratory and require confirmation in an adequately powered, randomized sample. The provisional instrument is described to support that work.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly performs the cognitive tasks that accounting ethics education has treated as central to ethical competence. This paper aims to reconceptualise ethical competence as ethical becoming, the ongoing formation of the dispositions and judgement required for answerable professional practice. Design/methodology/approach Through theory synthesis, the paper integrates virtue ethics, Vallor’s account of technomoral virtue, professional identity formation theory and socialising conceptions of accountability. Four practice scenarios set in South Africa’s International Financial Reporting Standards–based accounting environment illustrate the framework against a knowledge-transmission account of ethical competence. Findings Ethical becoming is expressed through practical wisdom, moral courage, relational accountability and situated professional judgement. Relational accountability grounds the other capacities, and situated professional judgement brings them together in decisions answerable to those they affect. The capacities develop through participation, rehearsal, reflective practice and mentorship within communities of practice, in an AI-enabled environment that can remove or open opportunities to exercise ethical judgement. Research limitations/implications The framework is conceptual and illustrated in one jurisdiction. Its four propositions require testing with students, trainees and practitioners. Practical implications The framework informs curriculum design, teaching and assessment, illustrated through a worked example, and supports professional bodies and organisations in building ethical formation into competency frameworks and workplace learning. Social implications Forming professionals who remain answerable to investors, communities and others affected by professional judgement strengthens the public trust on which accounting’s public-interest mandate depends. Originality/value Drawing on Vallor’s technomoral virtue ethics, this paper connects ethical formation and AI-enabled accounting, explaining how practical wisdom, moral courage and answerability form when AI performs part of professional work.

Environmental public service platforms are persuasive digital systems whose functions are critical for translating users’ short-term energy-saving actions into sustained energy-saving behaviors (SESBs), defined as consistent low-carbon practices across different contexts. Grounded in persuasive system design principles, this study employs the hierarchical regression, Necessary Condition Analysis (NCA), and fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) on 410 Chinese samples to examine how heterogeneous platform functions and their configurations relate to SESBs. Results show four platform functions (task-driven function, human–computer interaction (HCI) function, socialization-driven function, and system reliability feedback function) are positively associated with SESBs, yet none is a necessary condition. The HCI function serves as the core condition across all configurations. Three equifinal configurations for SESBs are identified: “interaction-enhanced task-trust driven mode,” “interaction-supported task-social synergy mode” and “interaction-empowered social-trust driven mode.” These findings offer platform operators insights into the relationship between functional configurations and users’ SESBs, providing empirical evidence for optimizing function design to promote energy conservation.

Personal health data spaces (PHDSs) promise to give individuals meaningful control over longitudinal health information while making heterogeneous data available across settings of care.The promise is consequential: continuity may improve when a person can authorize access to clinical records, patient-reported information, wearable data, and other sources without each transition requiring a new reconstruction of the record. Yet technical availability is not equivalent to continuity. A PHDS can be interoperable, secure, and formally patient-controlled while remaining difficult to use, weakly integrated into clinical work, or unevenly accessible. The central challenge is therefore not only to build PHDSs, but to implement them so that data become usable relationships and coordinated action.The articles in this Research Topic make that challenge visible from complementary directions. Ambalavanan et al. propose a modular, ontology-driven front-end architecture linking user experience, security, data management, interoperability, analytics, and scalability (1). Lin et al. describe a blockchain-supported dynamic consent framework through which participants can modify permissions and data uses over time (2). Ruan et al., studying a population at high risk of stroke, show that proactive health behavior is associated with health literacy, social support, self-efficacy, and material circumstances (3). Read together, these contributions suggest that a technically capable data space will produce continuity only through an implementation system that makes participation understandable, supported, actionable, and revisable.This Opinion argues for a responsive implementation approach to PHDSs, in which technical capabilities, governance arrangements, organizational workflows, user supports, and learning processes are deliberately connected to improve care continuity. The SPHERE model -Social Prescribing and Health Equity through Responsive Evaluation -was developed for policies enabling social prescribing, not for digital health architecture (4). Its value here is therefore not as a template to transfer wholesale. Rather, its eight-part logic offers a useful viewpoint: durable effects emerge when foundations, infrastructure, community co-production, context, implementation strategies, process measures, outcomes, and feedback loops are deliberately connected. Applying that logic to PHDSs shifts the evaluative question from whether a data space exists to how, for whom, under what conditions, and through which mechanisms it improves continuity, and how implementation should be revised as evidence and surrounding conditions change.PHDS discussions often separate technical design from "adoption," treating implementation as a downstream step. This division is misleading. Decisions about identity verification, consent granularity, provenance displays, terminology services, access delegation, and clinical integration distribute work and authority among patients, caregivers, clinicians, organizations, and data stewards. They are implementation decisions because they shape who can participate, what actions are feasible, and whether the technology fits existing routines. Frameworks such as the updated Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research and NASSS similarly emphasize that technologies interact with recipients, organizations, wider systems, and change over time (5,6). Human-factors approaches further show that outcomes arise from interactions among people, tasks, tools, organizational conditions, and environments rather than from any component alone (7).Ambalavanan et al.'s layered architecture illustrates the point (1). Semantic standards may allow data to travel and be interpreted consistently, while a patient-centered front end can make provenance, consent status, and longitudinal information visible. Yet a provenance indicator may increase trust when its meaning is clear, add burden when it is not, or be ignored when clinicians lack time to review externally generated information. The relevant unit of analysis is therefore the sociotechnical arrangement: the feature, the stakeholders expected to use or govern it, the workflow in which use occurs, and the authority and resources that make action possible.This framing also clarifies why care continuity should not be inferred from interoperability alone. Interoperability is a necessary capability, but continuity is an experienced and organizational outcome: relevant information is available at the right transition, interpreted in context, and used to coordinate a next step. Evaluation should trace that full pathway rather than stop at successful exchange. It should also examine the collective work through which PHDS use becomes routine: how participants make sense of the data space, enroll others in using it, perform the required tasks, and appraise its value over time (8). These processes may explain why the same technical capability becomes embedded in one setting but remains peripheral in another.SPHERE's contribution is to connect enabling structures with the work required to make them effective and accountable (4). Adapted cautiously, its components suggest four linked commitments for PHDS initiatives.First, align foundations and infrastructure. Legal authority, governance, financing, technical architecture, stewardship roles, and clinical accountability should be specified together. A right to access or control data has limited operational value if organizations are not responsible for ingesting, reconciling, and acting on authorized information. Conversely, an elegant architecture will remain fragile if consent, liability, secondary use, and cross-organizational responsibilities are unsettled. World Health Organization guidance likewise positions digital health as requiring coordinated governance, organizational capacity, and person-centered design, not technology in isolation (9).Second, co-produce the implementation system across stakeholder groups with distinct interests and forms of authority. Patients and caregivers have particular standing because the data concern identifiable persons and because PHDS choices can directly affect their autonomy, privacy, and care. However, healthcare professionals and provider organizations, payers and purchasers, researchers and public-health bodies, regulators and data stewards, and technology developers also create, use, finance, govern, or derive value from PHDSs. Their priorities may diverge: granular patient control can complicate clinical access; data availability for research can conflict with preferences concerning secondary use; documentation requirements can strengthen accountability while increasing workload; and short-term affordability decisions can constrain longer-term public benefit. A SPHERE-informed approach does not erase these tensions. It uses co-production to identify them, governance to clarify decision rights and accountability, and stakeholder-specific measures to examine how benefits, costs, risks, and work are distributed. Co-production should therefore encompass the surrounding service and governance pathway (not only the user interface) and should continue as evidence and conditions change (10).Third, specify strategies and measure implementation outcomes. Training, workflow redesign, facilitation, technical assistance, audit and feedback, and outreach are distinct strategies, not an undifferentiated implementation package. Each should be described by its actor, action, target, timing, dose, intended outcome, and rationale (11); established strategy compilations can support consistent naming while still requiring selection for local barriers (12). Early outcomes should include acceptability, adoption, appropriateness, feasibility, fidelity, cost, penetration, and sustainability (13), alongside population-specific reach and burden. These measures help distinguish a weak intervention from a strong intervention that is poorly implemented. They also prevent login counts or consent completion from standing in for meaningful use.Fourth, build feedback loops that connect implementation to continuity. PHDS initiatives should monitor not only system performance and security events, but also whether exchanged information changes care. Signals should include whether relevant data were available and reconciled, whether patients understood subsequent plans, whether duplicated work was avoided, and whether follow-up occurred. Quantitative patterns should trigger inquiry with users, nonusers, and other affected stakeholders; findings should then inform changes to interfaces, workflows, supports, governance, and implementation strategies. As Figure 1 illustrates, this is a recursive rather than linear process. Changes in legal requirements, medical knowledge, data availability, organizational relationships, or technology may require reconsideration of earlier assumptions and design choices. Responsive evaluation thus makes measurement part of governing and improving the system rather than a retrospective verdict and moves PHDSs toward a learning health system (14).Patient agency is central to PHDSs, but agency should not be reduced to the availability of settings, dashboards, or consent choices. Lin et al.'s dynamic consent framework appropriately treats consent as revisable rather than a one-time transaction and foregrounds traceability, withdrawal, and accountability (2). Its broader implementation implication is that control must be usable over time. People need to understand what a choice governs, anticipate its consequences, revisit it without undue burden, and obtain support when preferences or circumstances change. Supported agency should therefore be examined throughout design, implementation, and evaluation rather than treated solely as a property of the interface.Ruan et al.'s findings caution against designing for an abstract, self-sufficient user (3). Although their cross-sectional study did not evaluate PHDSs or establish causal mechanisms, its associations of active health behavior with health literacy, self-efficacy, social support, and material circumstances underscore that information availability does not ensure capacity to act. PHDS implementation should provide multiple routes to agency, including accessible interfaces, supported decision-making, safeguarded proxy access, assistance through clinical or community touchpoints, and non-digital alternatives where needed.Supported agency is also a health equity concern. Uniform access to a complex interface can reproduce health inequity when connectivity, language access, disability accommodations, institutional trust, time, or social support differ. Evaluations should therefore disaggregate reach, use, burden, and continuity outcomes and examine which groups are missing, withdrawing, delegating access, or experiencing unresolved data problems (15)(16)(17). Patient control is meaningful only when the practical conditions for exercising it are present.A PHDS evidence agenda should make five interrelated measurement dimensions explicit. First, technical performance measures (such as exchange success, semantic concordance, latency, provenance completeness, and security) show whether the infrastructure functions. Second, implementation measures assess whether people and organizations can and do use it. Third, mechanism-focused measures examine whether use changes comprehension, trust, supported agency, shared situational awareness, or coordination. Fourth, service and health outcomes test whether those changes improve continuity, timeliness, safety, experience, and health. Fifth, economic measures assess financial costs and the work or burden shifted among patients, caregivers, clinicians, organizations, payers, and other stakeholders. Findings in one dimension should be interpreted in relation to the others: technically successful exchange, for example, cannot establish benefit if the information is not incorporated into work or if doing so produces unsustainable burden.No single study must cover the entire chain, but programs should identify which links they are testing and avoid claims that cross unmeasured links. Dynamic consent may strengthen perceived control and trust, but these mechanisms and their downstream effects require prospective study (2). Semantic integration may improve information availability, while its usability and workflow fit require evaluation in practice (1). Mixed methods, pragmatic trials, longitudinal implementation studies, and comparative case studies can collectively establish what works, for whom, under which conditions, and at what cost. RE-AIM can additionally examine whether benefits extend across intended populations and settings and endure over time (18).Several frameworks could support PHDS implementation, and SPHERE should not be presented as uniquely capable of doing so. NASSS offers a technology-specific account of complexity across the condition, technology, value proposition, adopter system, organizations, wider context, and adaptation over time (6). CFIR provides a more detailed taxonomy of multilevel implementation determinants (5), SEIPS foregrounds interactions within work systems (7), and RE-AIM organizes population-and setting-level impact (18).
