The CeHRes Roadmap 2.0 more directly guides the intertwined development, implementation, and evaluation of eHealth technologies through continuous stakeholder involvement and formative evaluation (19). A recent review further found that NASSS has been used most often retrospectively and called for greater prospective and concurrent application during implementation (20).SPHERE's complementary contribution is its explicit connection of enabling foundations and infrastructure with co-production, implementation strategies, process and mechanism measures, outcomes, equity, and responsive feedback (4). This structure helps connect the five practical questions posed here (who benefits, what work is required, which strategies support that work, which mechanisms connect use to continuity, and what evidence should trigger revision) to specific parts of an implementation logic rather than treating them as a stand-alone checklist. Its limitations are equally important. SPHERE was developed for policies enabling social prescribing, has not been prospectively validated for PHDS implementation, and provides less technological and work-system detail than NASSS, CeHRes, or SEIPS. It is therefore best used as an orienting scaffold alongside, rather than in place of, frameworks selected for particular analytic tasks.For PHDS initiatives, the practical implication is to design implementation and evaluation with the data space and to revisit both over time.

BACKGROUND: Barcelona's municipal Home Care Services (HCS) have undergone a teamwork- and proximity-based reorganization aimed, among other goals, at improving workers' labor conditions. Although team-based home care has been commonly studied in relation to job satisfaction and autonomy, evidence on workers' physical health is limited. OBJECTIVE: To assess the impact of HCS reorganization on workers' employment conditions, ergonomic hazards, and physical health outcomes. METHODS: Mixed-method quasi-experimental pre-post design (2022-2024). Quantitative data included 1288 survey observations from intervention and comparison groups across three waves (pre: 550 workers; post1: 397 workers; post2: 341 workers). Qualitative data comprised 27 longitudinal interviews with intervention group workers at two time points, with one participant lost to follow-up. RESULTS: Quantitative descriptive results showed increased full-time employment and shorter travel times between users' homes in the intervention group. Ergonomic risk exposure was high across groups, but lifting or moving people augmented only among intervention workers. These workers also reported higher levels of fatigue and poorer self-rated health over time. Multivariable analyses confirmed results on travel times, exposure to lifting or moving people, and fatigue. Qualitative findings suggest sustained exposure to ergonomic hazards and indirect effects of the reorganization as potential mechanisms behind fatigue. CONCLUSIONS: Among intervention workers, three main changes were associated with the HCS reorganization: shorter travel times between users' homes, more frequent lifting or moving people, and higher fatigue levels. Further strategies are needed to reduce physical strain and safeguard workers' health in this essential care sector.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Chronic nonspecific low back pain (CNSLBP) is a leading cause of disability worldwide, while prolonged sitting, excessive screen time, and physical inactivity may contribute to persistent symptoms and functional limitations. This narrative review aimed to synthesize evidence regarding Pilates-based rehabilitation for CNSLBP in the context of increasingly sedentary lifestyles. A literature review was conducted using PubMed, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect, primarily covering publications from 2017 to 2026 and supplemented by seminal references. Eligible sources included original research articles, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical practice guidelines. Relevant publications were screened by title and abstract, assessed through full-text review, and supplemented by reference list searches. The reviewed evidence suggested that Pilates-based exercise could reduce pain intensity and disability while improving physical function, trunk muscle endurance and control, flexibility, body awareness, and health-related quality of life, particularly when compared with minimal intervention or educational advice alone. These benefits may be associated with improved trunk muscle activation, lumbopelvic motor control, breathing coordination, and confidence in movement. However, evidence regarding the superiority of Pilates over other active exercise interventions remained inconsistent, and the certainty of the available evidence varied across outcomes and comparisons. Pilates-based exercise may therefore represent a valuable component of multimodal rehabilitation incorporating ergonomic education, regular physical activity, reduced sedentary behavior, and biopsychosocial management. Further high-quality research is needed to standardize intervention protocols, determine optimal exercise frequency, intensity, and duration, and evaluate long-term functional outcomes and recurrence prevention among individuals with sedentary lifestyles.

Generative AI can support learning, but it may also encourage cognitive outsourcing by replacing learners’ own thinking. This study reframes AI from an information provider to a responsive listener that promotes cognitive engagement and self-explanation. We introduce Hearble, a minimal robotic listener designed to isolate the effects of different backchannel modalities. Using a between-subjects design, we compare four conditions: no response, visual, nonverbal acoustic, and verbal backchannels. We examine how these conditions affect utterance elaboration, cognitive load, immediate comprehension, knowledge transfer, and perceived agency. Rather than limiting AI intervention to preserving learners’ cognitive processes, we investigate whether AI can actively support them by encouraging learners to articulate and elaborate their own thoughts. This work presents the physical AI listener as an alternative interaction paradigm for learning and provides a controlled foundation for future research on how embodiment, facial expressions, gestures, and other audience cues shape learning and agency.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The increasing adoption of Artificial Intelligence by organizations has significantly transformed knowledge creation, sharing, and use processes. At the same time, challenges related to information quality, algorithm transparency, and accountability in decisions supported by intelligent systems have become more evident. In this context, this study analyzes the theoretical foundations of Knowledge Governance in Artificial Intelligence-supported environments and proposes a conceptual framework to understand the relationships among information, knowledge, technology, and human factors. This qualitative, exploratory, and descriptive research was developed through a narrative literature review with a structured search and conceptual analysis. The examined literature enabled the identification of recurring elements associated with governance, knowledge management, algorithmic ethics, and digital transformation. As a result, five analytical dimensions—strategic, informational, organizational, technological, and human—were systematized as the foundations of Knowledge Governance in contexts characterized by the growing use of intelligent systems. The proposed framework integrates these dimensions into a systemic perspective, highlighting that the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence depends not only on technological resources but also on information quality, organizational learning processes, and human-centered principles.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The Common Agricultural Policy (CAP) 2023–2027 replaces compliance-based oversight with a performance-based implementation model, supported by the Performance Monitoring and Evaluation Framework (PMEF), the Integrated Administration and Control System (IACS), and remote sensing-based monitoring. This shift primarily concerns the relationship between the European Commission and the Member States; conditionality and administrative controls at the farm level remain in place. This narrative synthesis, guided by PRISMA principles, examines how these governance and compliance mechanisms relate to farmers’ attitudes, trust, and behavior. It is based on a search of the Web of Science Core Collection and includes 81 studies. The studies point to a major institutional shift, the benefits of which are contingent upon an incomplete coherence across governance levels, while control and audit mechanisms are frequently described as sources of administrative costs and complexity. Institutional trust and perceived fairness emerge as explanations for farmers’ reactions; however, the evidence is largely attitudinal, pertains to earlier periods of the CAP, and does not test trust as a mediator. Findings regarding the erosion of intrinsic motivation are mixed. Digitalization may reduce administrative burdens, but its effect on the perceived opacity of compliance verification has not yet been examined among farmers. We propose longitudinal, farm-level research and comparisons between Member States in Central and Eastern Europe and other Member States.

This paper presents the teaching practices implemented in the course Introduction to World Economics to cultivate students’ higher-order thinking skills, covering aspects such as instructional design, teaching activities, and teaching evaluation. The instructional design is guided by Bloom’ s Taxonomy of Educational Objectives, and the teaching process is guided by the ARCS Motivation Theory. Ideological and political education is integrated into the course content through philological/documentary materials. Case-based teaching is the primary instructional method, and teaching evaluation draws on the Collegiate Learning Assessment+ (CLA+) model developed in the United States. The reconstruction and practical implementation of the course content for Introduction to World Economics, grounded in the cultivation of higher-order thinking skills, places greater emphasis on students’ intrinsic motivation to learn and offers a preliminary exploration of how to cultivate students’ higher-order thinking skills. Keywords: higher-order thinking skills; ARCS motivation theory; content reconstruction and practice

The aim of this study is to identify occupational health and safety risks faced by hospital employees and to comparatively analyze the Matrix and Fine-Kinney methods used in risk assessment. The study was conducted in a hospital located in Diyarbakır, and data were collected through on-site observations and structured checklists across different clinical units. Within the scope of the study, various hazards were identified, including infection risks, workplace violence, ergonomic issues, chemical exposure, and physical environmental factors. Based on the collected data, risk assessments were performed using both methods, and post-control residual risks were compared. The findings indicate that the Fine-Kinney method provides a more detailed and sensitive evaluation of risks, whereas the Matrix method offers a more general classification. Sharp object injuries, verbal violence, and inadequate ventilation were identified as the most critical risk factors. In conclusion, the use of systematic risk assessment methods is crucial for improving occupational health and safety practices in hospitals. This study contributes to the literature by comparing different risk assessment approaches and provides practical implications for effective risk management in healthcare settings
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Although environmental regulations can incentivize firms to reduce emissions, how firms adapt may depend not only on their organizational characteristics but also on the physical realities of their assets. This paper examines how multinational spread, an organizational feature in which firms own and manage similar production activities across countries, and the physical asset characteristics of production facilities jointly shape firms’ responses to carbon taxation. Using global, real-time satellite data on carbon emissions from 882 steel plants across 67 countries over 96 months (January 2015 to December 2022), we analyze operational adjustments firms can make to reduce carbon emissions: producing more cleanly by reducing emissions intensity of production or producing less by reducing asset utilization. We first examine how firms adapt to Canada’s carbon tax using a difference-in-differences (DID) design and then examine the impact of carbon taxes across countries using a stacked DID design. Our analysis reveals that, following Canada’s carbon tax, firms without multinational spread reduce carbon emissions primarily by lowering asset utilization; in contrast, firms with multinational spread additionally reduce emissions intensity of production. Importantly, our analysis of carbon taxes across countries shows that multinational spread alone does not dictate firm adaptation. Adaptation is fundamentally influenced by the physical technology on the ground: firms with multinational spread reduce emissions intensity of production and increase asset utilization at their clean (electric arc furnace) plants relative to dirty plants. Our study thus sheds light on how firms pursue different adaptation strategies at production facilities in response to carbon taxation.

Ritual spaces are integral to the architectural and cultural heritage of traditional Chinese villages. However, little is known about how their spatial morphology influences visual perception. This study investigated the relationship between spatial morphology and visual perception through an eye-tracking experiment conducted in 21 representative ritual spaces selected from 47 traditional villages in Yuxian County, China. 62 participants viewed three spatial types (point, linear, and areal). Data from 56 participants were analyzed using six eye‑tracking metrics and a 12‑item perceptual questionnaire. The results indicate that spatial morphology significantly affects visual attention and perceptual experience. Point spaces attracted the most concentrated visual attention and longest fixations, suggesting deeper cognitive engagement. Linear spaces promoted sequential visual exploration along spatial axes, whereas areal spaces encouraged dispersed attention and broader visual scanning. Point spaces also received significantly higher ratings for historical-cultural value and sense of place, particularly regarding cultural continuity, symbolic meaning, spiritual experience, and ritual atmosphere. Significant correlations between eye-tracking indicators and subjective evaluations further demonstrate the close relationship between visual behavior and spatial perception. These findings provide empirical evidence for understanding the perceptual effects of ritual-space morphology and offer practical implications for the conservation, design, and adaptive reuse of traditional village heritage.

Human factors and ergonomics (HFE) will inevitably face challenges arising from changing conditions, particularly technological developments. Six main challenges have been identified: Evolution of Societal Thinking; Future of Human Work in Industry 5.0; Climate Change and Sustainability; Future of Education and Training; Future of Personalized Health; and Life, Technology, and the Metaverse. Considering these challenges independently would be unrealistic, given HFE’s aim of ensuring human health and well-being. Therefore, this study analyzes their relationships using a two-stage approach. First, Decision-Making Trial and Evaluation Laboratory (DEMATEL) examines their mutual influences. Second, Interpretive Structural Modeling (ISM) identifies the driving forces and root challenges. The results indicate that Evolution of Societal Thinking influences three other areas, while Future of Human Work in Industry 5.0 and Future of Education and Training exhibit internal dependencies. Finally, the study discusses how these findings can help mitigate future HFE challenges.

Abstract We present the first application of spectral nudging in a probabilistic ensemble forecasting framework, combining the physics‐based European Centre for Medium‐Range Weather Forecasts' Integrated Forecasting System ensemble (IFS‐ENS) with forecasts from the probabilistic machine‐learned Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System Ensemble. Large scales of virtual temperature and vorticity are relaxed toward the machine‐learned forecasts, while mesoscale structures remain governed by the physics‐based model. This hybrid ensemble shows substantial improvements in large‐scale forecast skill, with gains in predictive skill extended by up to 2 days in the Tropics and by approximately half a day in the extratropics relative to IFS‐ENS. Despite nudging being applied only to upper‐air fields, improvements are also found in several near‐surface parameters. Tropical cyclone track forecasts improve significantly, consistent with improved representation of the large‐scale steering flow, without degrading storm intensity or ensemble spread. These results demonstrate that spectral nudging can be successfully extended to ensemble prediction and provide an attractive pathway for combining machine‐learned and physics‐based weather prediction systems.

The consolidation of Open Science has expanded the role of informational infrastructures in the production, circulation, and preservation of scientific knowledge, assigning persistent identifiers an increasingly central position in this ecosystem. This research investigates how the scientific literature has discussed the role of persistent identifiers in the context of Open Science through an exploratory literature review. A total of 342 records were retrieved from the Web of Science and Scopus databases, of which 125 formed the final corpus after screening. The analysis adopted an inductive strategy, resulting in the organization of studies into seven thematic macro-axes, discussed in three analytical blocks: conceptual and infrastructural foundations; articulation with FAIR principles, FAIR Digital Objects, and scientific workflows; and dimensions of governance, institutionalization, and scholarly communication. The results show that persistent identifiers have been progressively repositioned in the literature, from technical solutions to the problem of digital reference instability to structural components of complex sociotechnical infrastructures, whose effectiveness depends on institutional arrangements, governance models, and coordinated practices among actors in the scientific ecosystem. The study contributes to an integrated understanding of persistent identifiers as transversal infrastructure of Open Science, highlighting convergences, emphases, and analytical gaps in the literature.

Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) requires learning environments that connect conceptual instruction with authentic occupational practice. Access to workplaces, however, may be restricted by safety, cost, logistics, operational disruption and limited equipment. Immersive 360° video can represent real professional settings and support situated observation through head-mounted displays (HMDs), mobile devices or conventional screens. This paper presents a scoping review of immersive 360° video in TVET, workplace learning and related professional education. Guided by Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported in accordance with PRISMA-ScR, the review searched Scopus, ERIC, IEEE Xplore, SpringerLink and ScienceDirect and identified 200 records. Following deduplication and screening, 49 publications representing 47 study clusters were included. The review mapped occupational and geographical contexts, evidence types, access devices, interaction, guidance, feedback, assessment, gamification, reported outcomes and limitations. Health and care professions accounted for 23 publications (46.9%), while industrial, engineering and production contexts accounted for eight (16.3%). HMDs were the primary or sole access mode in 33 publications (67.3%), and 30 (61.2%) incorporated at least moderate interaction. Twenty-six publications (53.1%) reported empirical interventions or comparisons, although comparator designs and outcome measures varied considerably. The literature frequently reported positive outcomes for presence, engagement, satisfaction, confidence and perceived authenticity. Findings for knowledge, professional performance and transfer were less consistent: several pedagogically structured interventions produced favourable results, whereas other comparisons found outcomes similar to conventional video or instruction. The reviewed literature does not support attributing educational value to immersion alone. Guidance, meaningful interaction, explanatory feedback, reflection and connection with practical activity emerged as recurrent features of interventions reporting favourable outcomes. The review also identified an uneven evidence base, with a strong concentration in health-professions education and short-term evaluations, with relatively limited evidence from apprenticeships, authentic workplaces and safety-critical operations. Future research should prioritise workplace and safety-critical contexts, delayed assessment, authentic performance and transfer, transparent reporting of instructional design, comparative device evaluation and pedagogically purposeful gamification.
keywords: technical and vocational education and training

documents.abstract: Research on incumbent adaptation through alliances typically assumes that incumbents can entice partners to share proprietary knowledge in a new technology by offering access to valuable complementary assets. This assumption fits the commercialization stage of a new technology, when both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets hold high value. However, during the pre-commercialization stage—when proprietary knowledge in the new technology is valuable but incumbents’ complementary assets cannot yet be fully deployed to commercialize the new technology—this logic may not hold. We develop a framework that explains how stage-dependent shifts in the value of both proprietary knowledge and complementary assets alter the bargaining power between incumbents and knowledge-possessing firms, thereby reshaping the adaptive potential of alliances. Using data on the semiconductor industry during the emergence of nanotechnology, we found that alliances between semiconductor incumbents and nanotechnology-capable partners are less likely to form and, even when formed, are less likely to focus on the explicit transfer of proprietary knowledge in emerging nanotechnology. Moreover, these alliances are more likely to be structured as joint ventures, especially when the risk of knowledge leakage is heightened. Joint venture arrangements, in turn, impede semiconductor incumbents’ post-alliance nanotechnology invention more than contractual arrangements. Taken together, we develop insights into how incumbents may struggle to use alliances for adaptive learning during the pre-commercialization phase of a new technology.

The intensification of digital technologies and the advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) have transformed the processes of information production, circulation, and validation, increasing challenges related to disinformation, particularly in light of generative AI, capable of producing highly plausible synthetic content. This paper analyzes how these transformations interfere with the production and dissemination of disinformative content, discussing their implications for Information Science. Methodologically, the study is an exploratory theoretical essay based on bibliographic research and a qualitative approach, articulating the concepts of information and disinformation with the epistemological perspectives of Thomas Kuhn (2013) and Gaston Bachelard (1996), based on an interpretive model structured in three complementary axes. The findings indicate that disinformation results from the interaction between algorithmic mediation, the reconfiguration of knowledge legitimation mechanisms, and epistemological obstacles involved in information interpretation processes. It is concluded that addressing disinformation requires the development of critical competencies and an understanding of the sociotechnical processes that organize the circulation of knowledge in contemporary society.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Multicultural education in Hong Kong poses learning challenges. For example, non-Chinese-speaking (NCS) students and newly-arrived students (NAS) come from diverse linguistic backgrounds. However, existing interventions emphasise unidirectional instruction. This study addresses the gap by investigating how an interactive robot-assisted scenario (RAS) system can support Cantonese instruction in multicultural classrooms. We employ a mixed-method approach examining quantitative engagement measures and qualitative experiential data. We investigate how RAS intervention can influence the engagement and motivation of NAS and NCS students to learn Cantonese, and the impacts of RAS on the Cantonese proficiency outcomes of NAS and NCS learners. Findings reveal differential engagement patterns: NAS demonstrate improvements in behavioural engagement, while NCS students show a slight decline in cognitive engagement. This research contributes to human-agent interaction (HAI) by examining cross-cultural learning dynamics and providing preliminary insights for the development of multicultural educational technologies.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Background: Digital exclusion is a multidimensional and relational process shaped by interactions among individuals, technologies, institutions, and wider social structures. Research on digital exclusion has expanded significantly in recent years, largely due to the COVID-19 pandemic and the rapid digitalization of health, welfare, and public services. Yet, despite this growth, conceptualizations of digital exclusion remain fragmented, limiting a comprehensive understanding of how digital exclusion contributes to the creation or intensification of health inequalities. Objective: This hermeneutic review aims to develop an interpretive understanding of how digital exclusion has been conceptualized across diverse bodies of literature in relation to health inequalities. Methods: We conducted a hermeneutic review using keyword searches and snowballing across PubMed, Scopus, and supplementary sources published between January 2020 and July 2025. Analysis involved repeated reading, note-taking, and comparative interpretation of each text's disciplinary field, theoretical orientation, and underlying assumptions about how digital exclusion is framed in relation to health inequalities. Knowledge users contributed throughout to ensure the developing interpretations remained relevant to policy, practice, and lived experience. Results: Thirty-one publications were included, spanning multiple disciplines and theoretical orientations. Five interpretive frames were identified: (1) inequality, which conceptualizes digital exclusion as arising from unequal social, economic, and material conditions; (2) power and social injustice, which highlights how institutional rules, governance arrangements, cultural norms, and service pathways condition who is recognized or supported, showing how digital systems can reproduce existing social hierarchies; (3) life transitions, which illustrates how exclusion shifts during periods of disruption or change, emphasizing the fluctuating conditions and vulnerabilities associated with major life changes; (4) psychobehavioral, which focuses on psychological, cognitive, and emotional responses to digital demands; and (5) sociotechnical misalignment, which frames exclusion as arising when digital systems do not align with people's routines or everyday contexts. These interpretive frames show how digital exclusion is understood through different yet overlapping explanations that emphasize structural conditions, institutional practices, life circumstances, individual experiences, and service and system design. Conclusions: This hermeneutic review identifies 5 interpretive frames that integrate diverse disciplinary perspectives on how digital exclusion contributes to health inequalities. The frames clarify the multiple, intersecting processes through which exclusion is produced and reproduced, helping to explain its persistence and uneven impacts. Our findings highlight the need for future research that examines structural and institutional mechanisms alongside lived experience and for digital health policy and practice to move beyond access- and skill-focused solutions toward approaches that address the multiple and interacting causes of digital exclusion.

Abstract Machine learning is revolutionizing chemistry. Beyond the value of predictive models accelerating virtual screening, generative AI aims at enabling inverse design, reversing the compound-to-property prediction paradigm into property-to-compound generation. Chemists now have access to a rich AI toolbox for organic chemistry, including drug discovery. However, the application of these methods to inorganic compounds remains limited by the challenges posed by their intrinsic nature. This perspective analyzes how these challenges have been addressed, considering widely diverse systems ranging from molecules to crystals, including transition metal complexes and microporous materials. The analysis focuses on how generative AI methods have evolved toward data-representation-model pipelines that address the full complexity of inorganic compounds, including their chemical composition, geometry, symmetry, and electronic structure. Future directions, like benchmark standardization and the development of synthesizability metrics, are also discussed.

Abstract Background AI-driven clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) are increasingly being introduced to enhance clinical decision-making, yet their adoption in health care remains limited. Research has examined technical, organizational, and contextual barriers to adoption, but less attention has been paid to how knowledge, values, and responsibility around AI-CDSS are constructed and negotiated in practice. Objective This study examines how clinicians and AI experts make sense of AI-CDSS by reanalyzing qualitative interview data through a feminist and constructivist science and technology studies (STS) perspective. Whereas the original study examined informational needs, this reanalysis asks how participants construct relevant knowledge, evaluate the value of AI-CDSS, and negotiate appropriate use and responsibility in clinical practice. Methods The authors conducted a reanalysis of semistructured interviews held in 2024 with clinicians (n=8) and AI experts (n=8) in the Netherlands. The original study focused on informational needs for AI-CDSS. For this analysis, a deductive coding framework based on European Commission guidelines for trustworthy AI was first applied, and the material was then inductively reorganized into 5 empirical themes. Subsequently, feminist and constructivist STS concepts were used as sensitizing concepts in an abductive analysis, and these concepts were brought into dialogue with the empirical themes to examine the sociotechnical relations underlying participants’ accounts. Results Situated knowledge shows that the informational needs of clinicians are not universal but relate to their roles and specific clinical contexts, with understanding oriented less toward technical transparency than toward actionable guidance, relevance, and integration into decision-making. Standpoint theory illuminates differences between stakeholder priorities: clinicians emphasize information on how to use and act on AI outputs within existing workflows, whereas AI experts focus more on providing technical characteristics and performance metrics. Tinkering captures how clinicians experiment with AI systems in practice to develop situated, lay forms of expertise. Situated value highlights that perceptions of an AI-CDSS’s worth are relational, with clinicians valuing novel, context-sensitive insights and developers prioritizing performance metrics. Finally, response-ability reveals how trust and accountability are largely delegated to institutional structures, while clinicians report limited legal, organizational, and structural support to respond meaningfully to uncertainty or errors when using AI-CDSS. Conclusions Reanalyzing the same interview material through an abductive STS approach makes sociotechnical dimensions visible that were not the focus of the original analysis. Rather than treating informational requirements as universal or adoption as primarily a matter of technical performance and communication, the findings show how knowledge, value, and responsibility are constituted through situated professional practices and institutional arrangements. Processes and considerations regarding how clinicians make sense of AI-CDSS are not universal but are shaped by social, cultural, and institutional contexts. This analytical perspective underscores the need for context-sensitive, multistakeholder strategies to support meaningful and responsible AI adoption in clinical practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This project assessed the viability of the AI-GENIE methodological framework for the construction and validation of personality psychometric instruments in a Peruvian university population. Through a Monte Carlo simulation, 900 samples were generated using six large language models (LLM) and three temperature parameters, producing approximately 121,717 items that were refined using the AI-GENIE steps: Unique Variable Analysis (UVA), Exploratory Graph Analysis (EGA), and bootEGA. Following manual post-hoc refinement, the 23-item HEXACO-IA-P scale was constructed and administered to 252 students. Results demonstrated that AI-GENIE possesses remarkable viability, successfully recovering the six-dimensional theoretical structure with a Normalized Mutual Information index (NMI) of .942 and node stability exceeding .70 for most items. Nevertheless, limitations related to semantic redundancy, variability across LLM models, and linguistic bias in algorithm training were identified. It is concluded that, although AI-assisted automated item generation constitutes a promising tool for modern psychometrics, its implementation in Spanish requires expert human supervision, methodological adjustments, and rigorous empirical validation to ensure the validity and reliability of the developed scales.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as automated judges for AI-generated content, yet a single judge is unreliable and even a panel of judges leaves a hard residue: when judges disagree, majority voting simply discards the conflict instead of resolving it. We present JuryFlow, a disagreement-guided, human-in-the-loop multi-agent evaluation framework that treats inter-judge disagreement not as noise to be averaged away, but as a precise, claim-level signal indicating where an evaluation is uncertain. JuryFlow decomposes each candidate response into atomic claims, has a panel of heterogeneous judges assign per-claim verdicts, and builds a disagreement graph whose nodes are scored by verdict entropy and whose edges encode structural similarity between claims. A human acts as a structural guide, i.e., selecting which disagreement to resolve through a single, minimal intervention rather than re-labeling the response, after which the focal claim is re-evaluated, the correction propagates along graph edges and to historically similar cases, and is crystallized into reusable rubric entries that all judges inherit, making the evaluator progressively self-refining. To enable large-scale, reproducible benchmarking without human studies, we evaluate JuryFlow in an automatic configuration in which the focal selection is made by entropy ranking. On MT-Bench and LLMBar, JuryFlow improves agreement with gold labels over single-judge and majority-vote panel baselines, and ablations isolate the contributions of disagreement-targeted re-evaluation, propagation, and rubric induction. We contribute (1) a human-in-the-loop paradigm that recasts the human from labeler to structural guide, (2) the JuryFlow framework operationalizing it through a disagreement graph, focal re-evaluation, and closed-loop rubric induction, and (3) an evaluation protocol with ablations that isolate where the gains originate.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BackgroundCare work involves high emotional and physical labor, exposing workers to psychosocial stressors, ergonomic risks, and health problems, making job burnout and job engagement critical issues for the sustainability of care services.ObjectiveThis study examines multidimensional factors associated with job burnout and job engagement among care workers in Korea to inform improvements in working conditions and policy.MethodsUsing data from the 6th Korean Working Conditions Survey, this study analysed 550 wage-employed care workers. Random Forest analysis ranked factors across individual characteristics, job demands, job resources, and health domains; multiple linear regression analyses then estimated associations for the ten highest-ranked variables for each outcome.ResultsJob burnout was positively associated with job demands, including job stress and emotional instability, as well as health-related factors such as systemic fatigue. In contrast, job engagement was primarily associated with job resources, including job prospects and perceived value of work. Region of employment and economic conditions were associated with both outcomes, suggesting that environmental and economic contexts are each relevant to care workers' job experiences.ConclusionsJob burnout was primarily associated with job demands and health-related factors, whereas job engagement was primarily associated with job resources. These exploratory, cross-sectional findings identify physical and psychological health support, professional development and social recognition, and economic and regional working conditions as policy areas for further consideration. Longitudinal and intervention research is needed to establish temporal relationships and evaluate workplace or policy measures.

Hybrid work models are now focused on decentralized decision-making and increased flexibility within the organization, yet the benefits from it for the employees' well-being and work-life balance are increasingly constrained by technostress. This chapter is developed from the perspective of human resource management; it's a combination understanding of technostress in hybrid and AI-mediated work environments. The influence on job satisfaction, employee well-being, and work-life balance is shaped by conceptualizing technostress as both job demand and a psychological need obstacle by relying on Job Demands-Resource (JD-R) theory and Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Amplified technostress through increased monitoring, uncertainty, and perceived loss of control are set as contextual enhancers by systems enabled by Artificial intelligence. This chapter advances by outlining targeted HR policies and governance by providing a holistic conceptual framework, by translating theory into practice, and by using AI-enabled work design and human centered hybrid for managing technostress.

The expansion of chatbots in digital environments has reconfigured forms of interaction among individuals, institutions, and informational content, especially in contexts of information search, access, and circulation. Against this background, this study is guided by the following question: how do RAG-based chatbots act as devices for information mediation? The objective is to describe the Divulga-AI chatbot as an information mediation device, focusing on its sociotechnical configurations and how these affect its costs. The theoretical framework brings together discussions on information mediation and RAG chatbots. Methodologically, the research is characterized as qualitative and exploratory, combining bibliographic review, action research, and documentary analysis. The empirical material comprised two technical documents related to Divulga-AI - the configuration screen and the behavioral instructions assigned to the chatbot - and two exploratory question-and-answer tests. The results and discussion are organized into three axes: presentation of Divulga-AI and its architecture; sociotechnical configurations and information mediation; and documentary, operational, and economic costs in algorithmic mediation. The study concludes that the sociotechnical configuration of RAG-based chatbots constitutes a form of implicit information mediation, as it defines the conditions for information retrieval, selection, contextualization, traceability, presentation, and cost in digital environments.

Purpose This study aims to examine how institutional complexity is reflected in the literature on work integration social enterprises in the intellectual disability sector (WISEs-ID). This study synthesizes research on institutional conditions, organizational orientations and practices, and outcomes and employment experiences for people with intellectual disabilities (PWID). Design/methodology/approach Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses Extension for Scoping Reviews, this scoping review analyzes 17 articles published between 2007 and 2026 using theory-informed qualitative content analysis. Findings The review finds that literature on WISEs-ID mainly addresses employment outcomes and experiences of PWID, while organizational practices and institutional conditions receive less systematic attention. By synthesizing studies on business and financing, work design, support practices and employment experiences, the review shows that productive work emerges as a connecting point between support and financial viability, linking meaningful work for PWID to value creation and organizational sustainability. Research limitations/implications The study proposes a multilevel framework linking institutional conditions, organizational orientations and practices and outcomes and employment experiences of PWID. It identifies gaps in the theorization of institutional complexity and in comparative research across contexts and target groups and develops a future research agenda to address them. Practical implications The framework helps practitioners reflect on how support, productive work and financial viability are organized through business and financing, work design and support and evaluation practices. This framework also highlights the need for policies giving WISEs-ID sufficient flexibility to provide meaningful and sustainable employment. Originality/value The study responds to calls in social enterprise research to move beyond social–commercial duality by offering a multilevel framework that unpacks this duality in WISEs-ID and understands these organizations as institutionally complex and embedded.

Social media platforms generate large volumes of multimodal content during natural disasters that can support situational awareness and humanitarian decision-making. However, effectively analyzing both textual and visual information remains challenging due to weak cross-modal alignment, severe class imbalance, noisy user-generated data, and limited labeled samples. This paper presents a unified multimodal transfer-learning framework that combines a frozen DeBERTa-v3-base text encoder with a frozen ResNet-50 image encoder through a simple late-fusion strategy for crisis-related classification. The architecture projects the unimodal features into a common 256-dimensional space, concatenates them, and feeds the resulting representation into a lightweight multi-layer perceptron classifier. The framework is evaluated on all three official tasks of the CrisisMMD v2.0 dataset. Experimental results show an accuracy of 0.76 (macro-F1 = 0.74) on the informativeness task, 0.43 (macro-F1 = 0.39) on the humanitarian categories task, and 0.69 (macro-F1 = 0.64) on the damage severity task. The model performs relatively well on classes with distinctive multimodal signatures, while residual confusion remains on semantically overlapping or visually subtle categories. For the damage severity task, which is primarily image-based, the multimodal model achieves essentially the same performance as an image-only configuration, indicating limited contribution from text. The study also acknowledges that formal text-only and image-only ablation experiments under the same protocol were not conducted, so the precise benefit of fusion cannot be rigorously quantified. Overall, the work demonstrates that a computationally efficient frozen late-fusion architecture can serve as a practical and reproducible reference point for multimodal crisis informatics under the resource constraints typical of real-world disaster response.

OBJECTIVES: While ageing is often associated with retirement, many older women in northern Iran continue working in rice fields despite musculoskeletal pain. This study explored their pain experiences and how they cope with this condition. METHODS: Using a grounded theory approach developed by Strauss and Corbin, we conducted semi-structured interviews with twenty-two female rice farmers aged sixty years and older. Data analysis involved open, axial, and selective coding, with constant comparative analysis. FINDINGS: Analysis revealed five main categories: pain experience and disability, pain management and coping, social and economic factors, emotions and attitudes, and family impact. These categories informed a multilevel biosocial resilience model suggesting that resilience emerges through interactions across biocultural, socioeconomic, and structural domains. CONCLUSION: The findings highlight areas for further consideration in occupational health, healthcare access, and social protection. They also draw attention to the need for policies and research that strengthen formal support systems and reduce structural constraints that compel continued work despite pain. Context-specific adaptation and further research are warranted before broader recommendations can be made.

When a large language model supplies research annotations, the choice of model becomes an analytic degree of freedom. We ask how much that choice matters by putting 1100 task–occupation cells to nine models from three vendors and weighting their ratings with worker-reported task importance in the British Skills and Employment Surveys. Rankings are substantially more stable than levels: pairwise rank correlations range from 0.74 to 0.92, while the share of British jobs scoring above 0.5 ranges from under 0.1% to 38%. We therefore treat the rater as one dimension of a multiverse, reporting each rater-specific estimate and its range alongside a Rubin-style summary that incorporates their observed dispersion. The consequences depend on the downstream empirical design. A post-2022 pay gradient of –0.020 log points per interquartile range is negative under all nine raters, although it continues a pre-existing trend. In online vacancies, all nine raters initially produce negative post-2022 gradients; after teleworkability is given its own period path, seven produce significant positive coefficients, two produce small negative coefficients, and the pooled estimate is indistinguishable from zero. Neither application identifies an effect of generative AI. Validation against worker-reported AI use, competing exposure measures, assistant traffic and an independent task survey supports incremental predictive content validity and portability, but any bias shared across raters remains unidentified. The paper’s contribution is a procedure for exposing and carrying observed LLM-rater disagreement into empirical estimates.

documents.abstract: Small and medium-sized businesses need timely financial guidance, yet historical accounting logs record self-selected and often co-occurring business changes rather than randomized recommendations. We formulate this setting as observational policy ranking: from pre-decision financial information, a policy selects one of 34 ledger-derived business-change categories for a target financial KPI. Using 85,078 company-month observations from 7,505 firms, we introduce Covariate-Adjusted Residual Policy Learning (CAR-PL), an action-wise R-learner that operates directly on multi-hot logs and regularizes selection by observational support. We compare CAR-PL with an uplift T-Learner, a conservative contextual value model, a zero-shot LLM, and non-personalized references on company-disjoint held-out firms under a shared model-assisted scoring rule. CAR-PL has the highest Gross Profit point estimate (0.084), the T-Learner has the highest Revenue point estimate (0.085), and the contextual value model has the highest Quick Ratio point estimate (0.062). CAR-PL and the T-Learner are not statistically separated on either growth KPI in matched company-clustered comparisons, while CAR-PL selects 33–34 categories and produces less concentrated selections across the catalog. Outcome-model-only scoring retains the same KPI-level point-estimate leader or top pair, and category rankings remain similar when the all-zero treatment reference is replaced by the most common training co-action pattern. These findings support objective-specific ranking of SMB financial guidance from multi-action accounting logs.

Digital observatories constitute sociotechnical infrastructures designed for the production, organization, monitoring, and use of information, and may support participatory processes and decision-making. This study analyzes the temporal evolution and thematic structure of the literature on social participation in digital observatories from 2016 to 2025, adopting territorial intelligence as an analytical perspective. It is a descriptive bibliometric study based on records retrieved from the Web of Science and Scopus databases. The corpus comprised 652 articles analyzed using the Bibliometrix package and the Biblioshiny interface. The results show growth in the number of publications over the period analyzed and reveal four thematic clusters: data science and computational infrastructure; citizen science, participation, and governance; digital systems and monitoring; and public health and epidemiology. As an interpretive contribution, these clusters were examined through the lens of territorial intelligence, highlighting relationships among information production and management, technological resources, governance, knowledge mobilization, and the involvement of social actors. The findings indicate that the literature connects digital technologies, collaborative practices, and information processes across different observation and monitoring contexts, pointing to relevant relationships with the production of territorial intelligence.

The construction industry remains one of the most dangerous sectors globally, with West African workers facing particular risks due to labour-intensive methods and limited regulatory enforcement. No previous systematic review has synthesized evidence on compliance with occupational health and safety (OHS) standards among construction workers in West Africa. We searched PubMed, IEEE Xplore, EBSCOhost, Science Direct and Google Scholar for quantitative studies published from June 2001 to August 18, 2026. Studies required extractable data on occupational health and safety compliance outcomes. Quality assessment used the JBI critical appraisal tool for cross-sectional studies. Studies rated as high risk of bias were excluded. Twelve cross-sectional studies met inclusion criteria: seven from Ghana and five from Nigeria. No eligible low- or moderate-risk studies from the other 14 West African countries were identified through this review. PPE use, access and provision varied substantially with helmet use 16.9%, hard-hat use 34.1% and respirator use of 1.7% during relevant tasks. 54.5% respondents in a Nigerian study reported that they did not wear a mask for silica-dust exposure. Welfare facilities were severely neglected, with flushable toilets on only 14.3% of sites. Safety knowledge and training were often more favourable than behavioural measures, but these constructs were not treated as equivalent to compliance. A study found that lack of safety training and inconsistent PPE use were associated with occupational injury, but the causality was not established. Factors associated with poorer compliance included younger age, lower educational level, casual employment, physical barriers and the absence of a construction‑specific regulatory framework. Evidence from Ghana and Nigeria identifies heterogeneous gaps across OHS compliance-related domains, particularly selected PPE practices, organisational implementation and welfare-facility provision. Knowledge, training, PPE availability and PPE use should not be interpreted as interchangeable compliance measures. Standardised multicountry observational studies and evaluations of proposed interventions are needed. Trial registration This systematic review followed PRISMA guidelines and was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420250649740).

documents.abstract: Construction remains one of the world's most hazardous industries, with migrants comprising a substantial part of its workforce. Little evidence exists on occupational health disparities between migrant and non-migrant construction workers. This review compares occupational health outcomes between these two groups to inform equitable worker protection strategies. Following PRISMA guidelines, we systematically searched fourteen electronic databases and gray literature for studies published from January 1990 to May 2025. Eligible studies reported quantitative occupational health outcomes for both groups. Study quality was appraised using adapted Joanna Briggs Institute criteria and results were narratively synthesized. Thirty-eight studies across fifteen high-, upper-middle, and lower-middle-income countries were included, totaling 55,615 adverse health outcomes among migrant construction workers and 566,643 among non-migrant construction workers. Most studies were of low to moderate quality and were primarily conducted in high-income settings. Migrant construction workers experienced higher rates of fatal and general occupational injury than non-migrants. While migrants had excess risk for fatal falls, traumatic brain injury, heat-related mortality, and ocular trauma, they experienced lower all-cause morbidity and mortality. Patterns of non-fatal injuries, musculoskeletal disorders, mental health problems, and cardiovascular and metabolic disease were mixed. Occupational and structural factors significantly associated with morbidity and/or mortality among migrants included fewer years of employment and work experience, type of work, limited safety training and briefing attendance, and lower educational attainment. Associated socio-demographic and cultural factors included poor language proficiency, ethnicity, gender, risk-taking attitudes, and low awareness of workplace hazards; the role of age varied across studies. Migrant status is a significant determinant of occupational health in the construction sector. Strengthening labor protections for migrant workers and providing multilingual safety training are likely to reduce harm. Disaggregating occupational safety and health surveillance data by migrant status will further strengthen the evidence needed to protect the most at-risk construction workers. Registration: PROSPERO CRD42014009154.

documents.abstract: This article addresses issues related to ergonomics and human factors, outlining key areas of research within this field. It emphasizes the role of analytical and optimization methods in making the most appropriate decisions in complex situations. The study examines selected publications that incorporate operations research, where the human factor plays a decisive role. The text also provides brief descriptions of the research areas covered in these publications, illustrating their diversity. For each case, the specific subject matter is explored, along with its connection to the broader field of human factors research and the methodology based on operations research.

This study aims to analyze students’ responses, enthusiasm, engagement, and cooperation through the use of the digital educational game Educaplay Froggy Jumps to support learning motivation in social studies. This study employs a qualitative, descriptive approach, in which data were collected through observation, in-depth interviews with teachers and students, and documentation of students in class IX.5 at SMP Negeri 7 Makassar. Data analysis utilized an interactive model comprising data collection, data condensation, data presentation, and drawing conclusions. The results of the study indicate that the use of the digital educational game Educaplay Froggy Jumps successfully sparked curiosity and high enthusiasm, transformed conventional learning into an enjoyable learning experience, and fostered students’ intrinsic motivation. Furthermore, group-based game-based learning has been shown to enhance dynamic collaboration through the mechanisms of peer scaffolding and the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD). Thus, this digital medium is an effective alternative innovative learning strategy for addressing student boredom.

Background: Musculoskeletal conditions (MSCs) are an important cause of pain, disability and reduced productivity among informal-sector workers, particularly market traders exposed to prolonged standing, heavy lifting, repetitive movements, and inadequate rest breaks (da Costa & Vieira, 2010; Pega et al., 2021). This study determined the prevalence of MSCs and identified their sociodemographic and occupational determinants among traders in the Rumuokoro and Choba markets in Obio-Akpor Local Government Area, Rivers State, Nigeria. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional design was employed, and 300 traders were recruited aged 30 years and above with at least six months of trading experience through random sampling across the two markets. Data were collected using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaires that incorporated a modified Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire and sections on sociodemographic characteristics and occupational exposures. Data were analysed using IBM SPSS Version 25, with descriptive statistics, chi-square tests, and binary logistic regression at a 5% significance level. Results: The prevalence of musculoskeletal conditions was 81.7% (n=245), with the lower back (68.6%), knees (52.2%) and shoulders (44.5%) being the most affected regions. Almost half (45.3%) experienced pain daily, and 82.0% reported that pain interfered with their work. Significant sociodemographic associations were observed for gender (females: 86.2% versus males: 73.1%, p=0.012), age (p=0.001), education (p=0.001), body mass index (p=0.002), and family size (p=0.004). Occupational factors independently associated with MSCs included standing for seven or more hours daily (AOR=3.67, p=0.001), regular lifting of loads weighing more than 20 kg (AOR=2.95, p=0.027); taking regular work breaks was associated with lower odds of MSCs (AOR=0.38, p=0.004). Conclusion: Musculoskeletal conditions represent a substantial occupational health burden among traders in Obio-Akpor LGA, affecting most of the traders surveyed. Occupational exposures, including prolonged standing, heavy lifting and the absence of work breaks, were associated with MSCs. These findings highlight the importance of preventive ergonomic improvements at market level and access to appropriate healthcare services.

documents.abstract: Abstract Background Acute pesticide poisoning (APP) remains a global public health concern. Although developing countries use only a fraction of the pesticides produced worldwide, they bear a disproportionately high burden of pesticide poisoning. Pesticide use improves agricultural productivity by reducing crop losses, but it also poses substantial risks to human health. This study determined the prevalence, symptom distribution, and exposure-related risk factors for APP among pesticide handlers at a macadamia estate in Northern Malawi. Methods In this cross-sectional study, 144 eligible participants were selected using stratified random sampling. Data were collected through face-to-face interviews using a structured, pretested questionnaire after written informed consent had been obtained. The questionnaire captured: demographic characteristics, signs and symptoms of APP, and exposure-related risk factors. APP was defined using the World Health Organization APP case definition matrix. Associations between exposure-related risk factors and occupational APP were assessed using multivariable binary logistic regression. Results APP prevalence was 63.9% (95% CI: 56.1%–71.7%), and skin irritation was the most frequently reported symptom (58.5%). Exposure-related risk factors significantly associated with APP were secondary education (AOR = 11.56, 95% CI: 3.35–39.92, p < 0.001), drinking water while handling pesticides (AOR = 39.58, 95% CI: 3.07–509.80, p = 0.005), direct contact with pesticides (AOR = 5.84, 95% CI: 1.68–20.26, p = 0.005), and entering treated fields immediately after pesticide application (AOR = 5.13, 95% CI: 1.49–17.70, p = 0.01). Conclusions Nearly two-thirds of pesticide handlers at the estate met the case definition for APP, indicating a substantial occupational health burden. APP was significantly associated with secondary education, drinking water while handling pesticides, direct contact with pesticides, and entering treated fields immediately after pesticide application. To reduce occupational pesticide exposure, targeted behavioral safety interventions should strengthen safe pesticide-handling practices.
